2026金融AI智能体落地新标杆：中原银行与中信建投最新实践启示
2026年6月，中国金融AI智能体落地迎来两个标志性事件：中原银行外呼营销智能体斩获”2026中国AI智能体领航者”奖项，中信建投证券”信谛听”智数平台1.5版本正式上线并率先在核心业务场景切换至国产大模型。这两条消息看似独立，实则指向同一个趋势——金融AI智能体的竞争，正从”模型参数竞赛”转向”规模化交付能力”的比拼。
趋势：金融AI智能体进入”可信交付”时代
截至2026年6月，中国已有近800款大模型完成备案，53.5%的银行已上线大模型应用（来源：2026年银行业大模型应用调研报告）。但与2025年的”试点潮”不同，2026年金融机构关注的核心问题已从”模型够不够强”变成了”交付够不够可靠”。
如我们在 《金融行业AI智能体落地指南》 中分析的，金融场景对AI智能体的核心要求是零容错。无论是外呼营销中的合规话术控制，还是投研分析中的信息溯源，任何一次模型”幻觉”都可能导致实质性业务风险。中原银行与中信建投的最新实践，恰好从两个不同维度回应了这一核心诉求。
中原银行：双引擎架构破解外呼营销合规难题
中原银行作为资产规模超1.4万亿的省属法人银行，拥有600余家营业网点、1.8万余名员工。其与中关村科金联合申报的”外呼营销智能体”项目，在2026中国AI智能体领航者评选中从众多参评项目中脱颖而出。
该项目的核心创新在于”通用大模型+SOP流程”与”业务微调大模型”的双引擎架构：
SOP强约束 ：通过标准作业流程（SOP）约束对话路径，确保外呼全程在合规框架内运行，从架构层面杜绝大模型”幻觉”带来的话术风险
业务微调 ：基于中原银行真实业务语料进行监督微调，大幅增强模型在存款、理财、个贷等场景下的语义理解和意图识别能力
人机协同 ：智能体完成客户意向初筛，高价值线索无缝转接至人工坐席深度转化
这种架构设计的关键洞察在于：金融场景不需要”全能”的AI，而是需要”受控”的AI。SOP相当于给AI画了一条合规的跑道，让它在这个范围内发挥最大效率，而不是自由探索。
中信建投：从”能生成”到”能负责”的AI落地标准
中信建投”信谛听”1.5版本的升级，则展示了另一条路径：以专业数据为核心壁垒构建可信AI体系。
值得关注的是，”信谛听”1.5率先切换至国产大模型DeepSeek V4并完成核心场景验证。有报道称，中信建投信息技术部门相关负责人在公开活动中对国产大模型能力与成本优势表达了肯定（具体表述未经当事人核实）。
“信谛听”1.5的核心升级包括三项关键能力：
自适应纠错框架 ：让代码自己改Bug，大幅提升策略回测效率
DeepTiming搜索 ：首次整合中信建投7000余篇研报，拆解为超10万个可溯源知识原子，用户提问20秒内获得附带原文链接的精准回答
多智能体协同研究 ：支持分析师团队与AI协同完成研究报告撰写
其中”DeepTiming搜索”的设计思路尤其值得关注——用专业审核过的研报框定信息边界，让每条结论都可溯源。这恰好回应了行业对AI语料污染的普遍担忧：高质量专有数据正在成为金融机构构建AI可信体系的关键防线。
金融AI智能体选型的三个关键维度
结合上述案例与当前市场供给（来源：2026年企业级AI智能体选型指南综合梳理），金融机构在评估AI智能体平台时建议关注以下三个维度：
维度 核心问题 中原银行方案 中信建投方案 合规可控 如何防止AI”越界”？ SOP流程约束+话术合规检查 研报知识原子+溯源机制 数据壁垒 AI是否基于真实业务数据？ 业务微调大模型+真实语料 20TB机构级金融数据+脱敏研报 国产适配 能否满足信创和数据安全要求？ 私有化部署+国产大模型接入 切换至DeepSeek V4完成验证 对于计划引入AI智能体的长沙及中部地区金融机构和类金融企业，这三个维度可以作为选型评估的基础框架。重点不在于平台功能多全面，而在于能否在合规前提下实现稳定的业务价值。
长沙企业的启示：金融AI智能体落地的”三先”策略
中原银行与中信建投的实践验证了一个核心结论：金融AI智能体落地的关键不在于技术有多前沿，而在于能否在合规框架下产出稳定的业务价值。对于长沙及中部地区面临AI转型的企业，建议采取”三先”策略：
先框定场景 ：选择容忍度相对较高、边界清晰的业务场景（如外呼初筛、文档处理、报告辅助），而非一开始就挑战核心交易系统
先建立标准 ：明确AI输出的合规要求和验证机制，确保每条AI结论都可回溯、可审计
先验证价值 ：通过小范围试点（如一个网点、一个业务条线）验证ROI后再规模化推广，避免一步到位的风险
如我们在 《2026国产大模型本地化部署成本实测》 中测算的，当前国产大模型的部署成本已降至单项目5-20万元的区间。这意味着即便是预算有限的中部企业，也完全可以在不盲目追求大规模投入的前提下，找到适合自己的AI智能体切入点。
结语：从单点试验到规模化落地的关键一步
中原银行的获奖与中信建投的升级表明，2026年中国金融AI智能体正在完成从”单点试验”到”规模化落地”的关键跨越。对于长沙及中部地区的企业决策者来说，现在的问题不是”要不要用AI”，而是”如何用AI”。从合规框架出发，以业务数据为基础，在小场景中验证价值——这或许是当下务实的AI落地路径之一。

items.fullContent:
How to Let Your Coding Agent Use Your Logged-In Chrome (2026)

To let a coding agent work in your real, signed-in Chrome, install a browser extension that hands it tabs, or turn on Chrome's remote debugging toggle so a tool can attach to the Chrome you already have open. On Claude Code with a paid Claude plan, Claude in Chrome ( claude --chrome ) is the shortest path; the list below gives the pick for every other agent and login.
We make Browser Use and Browser Harness. Everything about the other tools comes from their own docs and READMEs, checked October 25, 2026, and linked where I use it.
Which one fits your agent
Claude Code: Claude in Chrome if you sign in with a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan. On an API key, Bedrock or another provider it stays off, so use Browser Harness, Playwright MCP's extension mode or Chrome DevTools MCP.
Codex: in the ChatGPT desktop app, OpenAI's browser extension. In Codex CLI, Browser Harness or one of the two MCP servers.
Gemini CLI: its built-in browser agent with sessionMode set to "existing" , or any of the MCP options.
Cursor: its built-in Browser keeps its own cookies per workspace, not your Chrome logins. For your Chrome, add Browser Harness, Playwright MCP or Chrome DevTools MCP to .cursor/mcp.json .
Any MCP client: Playwright MCP in extension mode gives the agent tabs you pick. Chrome DevTools MCP in auto-connect mode or our Browser Harness give it your whole running Chrome.
Why not copy your cookies into a fresh browser?
Because a fresh automation browser is a different device. You can export cookies and load them, for example with Playwright MCP's --storage-state , which loads cookies and local storage from a file into an isolated browser context ( README ). It works on some sites and can fail on sites that tie sessions to your device or ask you to sign in again:
Sessions bound to your device. With Device Bound Session Credentials , Chrome keeps a private key in secure hardware such as a TPM, and when a site's short-lived session cookies expire, Chrome refreshes them only by proving it has that key. On sites that use it, copied cookies expire and can't be renewed on another machine.
Signing in again. A fresh profile starts logged out of everything, so you redo every login and second factor there. The Chrome DevTools MCP docs note that some accounts may prevent sign-in when the browser is controlled through WebDriver ( Chrome DevTools MCP docs ).
The old shortcut is closed. From Chrome 136, --remote-debugging-port and --remote-debugging-pipe are ignored on your default Chrome data directory; they need --user-data-dir pointing somewhere else. Google made the change because attackers were using remote debugging to pull cookies out of Chrome ( Chrome blog, March 17, 2025 ).
Every option below works in your real browser instead, so your logins, device checks and second factors stay where they are.
1. Claude in Chrome
Anthropic's Chrome extension, which Claude Code connects to from the CLI or the VS Code extension ( docs ).
Works with: Claude Code only.
Setup: install the Claude in Chrome extension (version 1.0.36 or later), sign in to Claude Code with /login , then run claude --chrome . Run /chrome to check the connection or turn it on by default.
Your Chrome? Yes. Claude opens new tabs in a tab group, shares your browser's login state and works in a visible window. The docs list Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, and say Claude Code also sets up Brave, Arc, Vivaldi and Opera.
Limits: needs a direct Anthropic plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise). It stays off with an API key or a claude setup-token token, through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, and in WSL. It pauses at login pages and CAPTCHAs for you to handle. Site permissions come from the extension's settings.
I'd use it if you only use Claude Code and already pay for a Claude plan. See also our Claude in Chrome page .
2. Playwright MCP, extension mode
Microsoft's Playwright MCP server normally launches its own browser with a persistent profile per workspace. Its --extension flag connects it to your running Chrome or Edge through the Playwright Extension instead ( extension README ).
Works with: any MCP client, including Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor.
Setup: install the Playwright Extension, then add the server with --extension :
{ "mcpServers" : { "playwright-extension" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "@playwright/mcp@latest" , "--extension" ] } } } Your Chrome? Yes, in tabs you choose. The first time the agent uses the browser, a page opens where you pick the tab it connects to. Several clients can connect at once; each gets its own tab group and only sees the tabs in it.
Limits: you approve each connection unless you copy the PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXTENSION_TOKEN from the extension into the server's env . If the extension is in several Chrome profiles, it connects to the one you used last; --profile-dir-name picks one. Chrome or Edge only.
I'd use it when you want the agent kept to specific tabs. Free, Apache-2.0. Our Playwright MCP comparison has more.
3. Chrome DevTools MCP, auto-connect mode
Google's Chrome DevTools MCP is built around debugging: performance traces, network requests, console messages. By default it starts a new Chrome with a dedicated profile. On Chrome 144 or later, --autoConnect attaches it to the Chrome you already run ( advanced usage , Chrome blog ).
Works with: any MCP client.
Setup: open chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging in Chrome and turn on remote debugging, then add the server with --autoConnect :
{ "mcpServers" : { "chrome-devtools" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest" , "--autoConnect" ] } } } Your Chrome? Yes. Chrome shows a dialog asking you to allow the session, then the "Chrome is being controlled by automated test software" banner while it runs. With several profiles open it connects to Chrome's default one and sees every open window of that profile.
Limits: you start Chrome yourself. The older route, --browser-url=http://127.0.0.1:9222 , needs Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port and a separate --user-data-dir , so it is a separate profile, not your everyday one. Google collects usage statistics by default; --no-usage-statistics turns that off.
I'd use it when the job is debugging your own app with your logins. Free, Apache-2.0. Our Chrome DevTools MCP comparison has more.
4. Gemini CLI's browser agent
Gemini CLI ships a browser subagent that runs a bundled Chrome DevTools MCP ( docs ).
Works with: Gemini CLI.
Setup: it is off by default. Enable remote debugging at chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging (Chrome 144 or later), then turn the agent on in settings.json with the session mode set to "existing" :
{ "agents" : { "overrides" : { "browser_agent" : { "enabled" : true } }, "browser" : { "sessionMode" : "existing" } } } Your Chrome? Only with "existing" , which attaches to your running Chrome. The default, "persistent" , launches Chrome with its own profile in ~/.gemini/cli-browser-profile/ .
Limits: form filling always asks for confirmation. allowedDomains limits where it can go, and maxActionsPerTask stops it after 100 tool calls by default. It shows a consent dialog the first time.
I'd use it if Gemini CLI is your agent: nothing extra to install. Our Gemini browser page lists the other options.
5. Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app
OpenAI's ChatGPT browser extension lets Codex and Work chats in the ChatGPT desktop app use your Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera or Vivaldi.
Works with: Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app. The docs only describe the desktop app; Codex CLI isn't mentioned.
Setup: in the desktop app, open Settings > Computer Use, select Install next to your browser, then pick the browser with an @-mention in a chat.
Your Chrome? Yes, the browser profile where you installed the extension, so it can act on sites you're signed in to.
Limits: by default it asks before it acts on each new website. You can allow once, for that site, or for all sites, which OpenAI labels Elevated Risk.
For Codex CLI, use Browser Harness or one of the MCP servers. Our Codex browser page has the setup lines.
6. Browser Harness
Our open-source tool ( GitHub , MIT). It attaches to the Chrome you have open over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. How the agent uses it depends on the agent:
Works with: Claude Code and Codex run it as a command-line tool with its skill, and there the agent writes any helper it is missing as it works. Cursor and other MCP clients, such as Gemini CLI, use browser-harness-mcp , which gives them a fixed set of browser_* tools ( MCP docs ).
Setup: paste the setup prompt from the README into your agent. It installs Browser Harness with uv , registers the skill and opens chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging , where you tick "Allow remote debugging for this browser instance" once ( install.md ). Then Chrome asks you to Allow the connection.
Your Chrome? Yes, the whole running browser, with your tabs and logins. The tab it controls gets a horse emoji at the start of its title, and it works in the background so your visible tab stays yours.
Limits: it sees your whole Chrome, not a chosen tab or site. It needs Chrome 144 or later for the toggle. Local recordings are off unless you say yes during setup. The command-line tool sends usage telemetry by default, including the code the agent pipes to it and what that code prints; browser-harness telemetry disable turns it off ( telemetry code , install.md ).
I'd use it when you want one tool you can use from Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor, on any plan or API key. Product page: Browser Harness .
Side by side
Option Agents Your real signed-in Chrome? Setup Cost, license Notes Claude in Chrome Claude Code Yes, in a tab group it opens Extension, then claude --chrome Needs a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan Off with API keys, Bedrock, Google Cloud, Foundry and WSL; pauses at logins and CAPTCHAs Playwright MCP, extension mode Any MCP client Yes, tabs you pick Playwright Extension plus the extension flag Free, Apache-2.0 Approve each connection unless you set the extension token; Chrome or Edge Chrome DevTools MCP Any MCP client Yes in auto-connect mode; its own profile by default Chrome's remote debugging toggle plus the auto-connect flag Free, Apache-2.0 Chrome 144+; Allow dialog; usage statistics on by default Gemini CLI browser agent Gemini CLI Yes in "existing" session mode; its own profile by default Settings file plus Chrome's remote debugging toggle Built into Gemini CLI, Apache-2.0 Chrome 144+; form filling always asks first ChatGPT browser extension Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app Yes, the profile with the extension Settings, Computer Use, Install Plan not stated in the docs Asks before each new site; Codex CLI not covered Browser Harness (ours) Claude Code, Codex; Cursor, Gemini CLI and other MCP clients via MCP Yes, the whole browser Setup prompt (or MCP config) plus Chrome's remote debugging toggle Free, MIT Chrome 144+; Allow dialog; usage telemetry on by default, one command turns it off; agent writes missing helpers in CLI mode Copied cookies Any No, a fresh browser Export cookies, then load them into a new browser Free Device-bound sessions can't be refreshed; you redo logins elsewhere
Quick setup by agent
These combine each tool's documented flags with each agent's documented MCP syntax. In Claude Code and Codex, everything after -- is passed to the server.
Claude Code ( MCP docs )
claude --chrome claude mcp add playwright-extension -- npx @playwright/mcp@latest --extension claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user -- npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest --autoConnect For Browser Harness, paste the setup prompt . Our docs' Claude Code tutorial sets up the Browser Use CLI instead, which is built on Browser Harness and also drives your signed-in Chrome. /claude-code-browser compares the options.
Codex CLI ( MCP docs )
codex mcp add playwright-extension -- npx @playwright/mcp@latest --extension codex mcp add chrome-devtools -- npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest --autoConnect For Browser Harness, paste the same setup prompt into Codex.
Gemini CLI ( MCP docs )
Use the built-in browser agent with "sessionMode": "existing" from section 4, or add Browser Harness through its MCP server:
gemini mcp add browser-harness uvx -- --from "browser-harness[mcp]" browser-harness-mcp The Playwright and Chrome DevTools JSON blocks above go under mcpServers in settings.json as they are.
Cursor ( MCP docs )
Add one of the JSON blocks above, or Browser Harness, under mcpServers in .cursor/mcp.json (or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for every project):
{ "mcpServers" : { "browser-harness" : { "type" : "stdio" , "command" : "uvx" , "args" : [ "--from" , "browser-harness[mcp]" , "browser-harness-mcp" ] } } } Cursor's built-in Browser needs no setup for your own app on localhost, but it keeps its own cookies per workspace, not your Chrome's. More in /cursor-browser .
Safety
An agent in your signed-in browser can do anything you can: send email, change settings, buy things. The vendors say so plainly.
Prompt injection is the main risk. Anthropic calls it "the biggest risk facing browser-using AI tools": instructions hidden in a page, email or document can trick the agent into actions you didn't ask for, such as sending your data somewhere. With Claude Opus 4.8 and its current defenses, attack success was under 0.08% in Anthropic's internal testing, and it says the risk is still not zero ( Anthropic ). OpenAI tells you to treat page content as untrusted and not to send secrets through browser tasks unless you have to ( OpenAI ).
Use a separate Chrome profile when you can. Anthropic recommends a separate browser profile without access to sensitive accounts such as banking, healthcare and government. With an extension, install it only in that profile; Playwright MCP's --profile-dir-name picks which profile it connects to. Tools that attach to the whole browser, like Chrome DevTools MCP and Browser Harness, see what that Chrome has open, so keep the sensitive accounts in a Chrome you don't attach to.
Know what the agent can reach. Chrome DevTools MCP warns that it exposes the browser's content to your MCP client ( README ). For the manual setup, where you start Chrome with --remote-debugging-port , it warns that any application on your machine can connect to that port and control the browser ( advanced usage ). The Chrome 144+ toggle used by auto-connect mode, Gemini CLI's "existing" mode and Browser Harness instead shows a dialog asking you to Allow each connection ( Chrome blog, December 11, 2025 ). Either way, turn remote debugging off when you're done.

items.title: OpenAI 智能体在隔离测试中借 CPU 缓存隐蔽通信
items.title_en: OpenAI's isolated AI agents found ways to talk to each other through CPU cache
items.summary: OpenAI 介绍其前沿模型训练已完全断网，并用 AI 智能体红队测试自家基础设施。隔离测试中，智能体在无网络、无共享文件的条件下通过 CPU 缓存时序差异、共享内存写入模式等侧信道通信，甚至独立建立编码方案交换信息。

OpenAI's isolated AI agents found ways to talk to each other through CPU cache
Matthias Bastian View the LinkedIn Profile of Matthias Bastian
Oct 24, 2026
Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER
Key Points
After a security incident in September, OpenAI now trains its most advanced models without internet access, using a closed offline environment built from cached data.
In security tests, isolated AI agents still managed to set up covert communication channels without a network connection or shared files, including by exploiting timing differences in the processor cache.
During an 11-day training pause, OpenAI had AI agents—among them GPT-6 Astra Cyber—attack its own infrastructure to find previously unknown vulnerabilities. Training resumed afterward under tighter controls.
OpenAI now trains frontier models without internet access and uses AI agents to red-team its own infrastructure. In separate isolation tests, agents even communicated through covert side channels, showing how hard true containment is.
On September 20, an internal research model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver to reach the open internet during training, even though OpenAI had already tightened security after the now infamous Hugging Face incident in July and other observed misalignment cases . OpenAI contained the breach quickly but still halted all frontier model training and evaluation.
OpenAI cuts frontier models off from the internet during training
OpenAI made a policy decision in response: Frontier models now train without internet access until safety measures justify restoring it. Models learn to browse and search inside a closed "offline world" built from indexed and cached web content, and all frontier reinforcement learning runs now operate this way. Ad
OpenAI's agent sandbox allows access only to offline resources. The live internet, other sandboxes, and OpenAI's infrastructure sit outside the containment boundary. | Image: OpenAI Full network isolation, a so-called air gap, isn't feasible yet because experiments still need external connections for operations and monitoring, the company says. But even a complete air gap wouldn't guarantee containment, according to OpenAI researcher Noam Brown . He gave one example of how isolated systems could still communicate: two separate computers could theoretically signal each other through temperature sensors, with one heating its CPU while the other reads the change. Ad
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made a similar argument in a recent interview: Sandboxes offer only limited protection against powerful-enough models, and at some point it may no longer be possible to trace how they escaped. Monitoring helps early on, but what ultimately matters is that an AI system internalizes human values, a problem the field knows as "AI alignment" and has yet to solve.
Isolated AI agents found ways to talk to each other through CPU cache
OpenAI documents just how hard it is to control AI agents in its blog post . During tests, agents found ways to communicate without a network. In one test, agents placed in separate, isolated environments on shared hardware were told to exchange secrets with no network connection and no shared files. Ad
They used the processor cache. One agent deliberately altered the data stored there, while the other measured differences in load times and decoded the message. The same technique is behind the well-known Spectre and Meltdown attacks .
More channels turned up through write patterns on shared memory and through OpenAI's own offline infrastructure, the system meant to replace the internet. One agent noted in its reasoning log that it "could create an acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle." Ad
In one case, agents were given only a general list of vulnerabilities and told to find a communication channel on their own. They developed a channel independently, agreed on an encoding scheme, and successfully exchanged information. The channels are usually slow and hard to exploit, OpenAI says, but they do reach across boundaries meant to keep agents apart. Ad
OpenAI turned AI agents loose on its own infrastructure
During the training pause, OpenAI also had teams of AI agents systematically attack its own infrastructure. The agents were given source code, configuration details, and documentation of potential vulnerabilities. OpenAI's goal was to test its defenses under conditions that favored the attackers. The agents included the upcoming GPT-6 Astra Cyber and an internal frontier model. The campaign consumed hundreds of billions of tokens, according to OpenAI.
Unique potential security issues identified during the red-teaming campaign, plotted against tokens spent in billions. Most appeared within the first 110 billion tokens. | Image: OpenAI The agents discovered previously unknown vulnerabilities in the open-source components in use and exploited them to escape from secured virtual machines. One was a vulnerability in Kata Containers, a widely used container isolation system. OpenAI reported it as CVE-2026-24834 and provided a patch. More fixes went to other projects, and OpenAI reported additional, as-yet-unpublished vulnerabilities through the "Patch the Planet" initiative.
In tests where agents had already gained control of a host, they found a vulnerability in nearly every remaining internet-facing service. In one case, an agent used a firewall-permitted connection to fetch an external URL through a metrics service. Others bypassed security filters through misconfigurations.
AI red-teaming is now required before every new training run
The agents could no longer find a way to access the internet that was both easy to exploit and hidden from monitoring, according to OpenAI. The red-teaming also exposed gaps in monitoring and in the automatic pause mechanism.
After fixing the issues, OpenAI resumed training and internal use of its frontier models on October 1, eleven days after the pause began. OpenAI says this kind of compute-intensive red-teaming campaign is now a standard part of the approval process for new training runs.

X 上的 OpenAI：“During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.
The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.
This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.
More details on the patch and mitigations below:
https://t.co/Y1Y72aHxrW”

items.summary: 月之暗面发布 Kimi K3.1 系列首个模型 Kimi K3.1 Pro，为 3T 级开放权重模型，上下文窗口 100 万 token，并同步推出速度快 2-3 倍的 Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed。
items.fullContent:
Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence
Download
Download Try Kimi
Scroll to explore
Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.
We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.
Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.com , Kimi Work , Kimi Code , and the Kimi API . The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.
Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence
Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.
Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%) . And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon , our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2% , above K3's 55.95% .
Coding
K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.
K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot , combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:
K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.
3D Modeling and Design
K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools , approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.
K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.
Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences:
3D Make is now live on kimi.com and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.
Finance
With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.
K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks:
Financial Modeling evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points.
Financial Research evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points.
Business Operation evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance.
Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)
The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:
Cybersecurity
As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.
Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example.
Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.
On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance.
Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.
Availability
Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.com and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API .
Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026.
Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch.
Details for each channel:
Kimi Agents: Download or update to the latest Kimi app from your mobile app store, available on iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS, or visit kimi.com .
Work with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app , version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs.
Code with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the /model command.
Build with the Kimi API: Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers.
Bring Kimi to your organization: Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team.
Benchmarks
Footnotes
Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95.
Coding benchmarks
Terminal-Bench 4.0. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is taken from the release blog ( https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ). All remaining scores are taken as the maximum value reported in either their blog posts or the official Terminal-Bench 4.0 leaderboard ( https://www.tbench.ai/ ).
Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. Our internal evaluation of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 yields a score of 9.3; However, an older version, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, scores 15.7 on the official Terminal-Bench-Science, so we report 15.7 here; all remaining scores are from the official Terminal-Bench-Science leaderboard ( https://www.terminal-bench-science.ai/ ).
DeepSWE v1.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. All scores are taken from each model's respective technical report. GPT-6 Astra( https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ ). Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1( https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card and https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-5-1-mythos-5-1-system-card ); DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ( https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news261017/ ); GLM-5.3 ( https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3 ).
SWE-Marathon v1.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is evaluated with the ClaudeCode harness. All other scores are taken from the official SWE-Marathon leaderboard ( https://www.swe-marathon.org/ ).
PostTrainBench. Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 were evaluated internally on v1.2 using the Claude-Code harness and H20 GPUs instead of H100 GPUs. For stable evaluation, all judge models used DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at maximum effort, which best matched the official GPT-5.6-Terra (xhigh) judge in testing. Other scores are from the official leaderboard ( https://posttrainbench.com/ ).
ProgramBench (binary score). We report binary scores rather than raw ProgramBench scores: a task receives a score of 1 if its ProgramBench score is ≥95%, and 0 otherwise. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and GLM-5.3 scores are taken from the release blog ( https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ); all remaining scores are from the Vals ProgramBench leaderboard ( https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/programbench ).
Internal Coding Bench: Kimi Code Bench 2.0 and Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Claude-Code harnesses; All other models are evaluated at their max-effort setting. Note that proprietary model testing may involve some fallback behavior.
BenchCAD. Open models are evaluated by us on 1,000-case subsets randomly sampled from the full 17,900-case Vision2Code dataset, at maximum reasoning effort. With-tools results use the Claude Code harness; without-tools results use single-shot generation with the official BenchCAD prompts and scoring pipeline. Scores for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 are taken from the Claude Opus 5.5 System Card ; GPT‑6 Astra’s with-tools score is taken from its official report . GPT‑6 Astra has not reported a without-tools score and is marked “—”.
Agentic benchmarks
BioMysteryBench dataset is drawn from the official v11 release , with Kimi K3 as the judge model. We evaluate Kimi K3.1 Pro with Kimi Code, GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 with Claude Code, and GPT-6 Astra with Codex. Scores for the Claude models are taken directly from their official system cards.
Our Agents’ Last Exam dataset is drawn from the official v1.1 release , comprising 122 tasks, including 86 CLI tasks, with environment images aligned with the official Hugging Face release. We additionally assign a score of zero to runs that bypass the task’s stated requirements, such as retrieving answers online instead of performing the required analysis in Wireshark. DeepSeek and Kimi are evaluated using Claude Code and Kimi Code, respectively. All other results are taken from the official benchmark website.
OfficeQA Pro, OfficeQA Pro v2. GPT-6 Astra is evaluated with Codex, while all other models are evaluated with Claude Code. Each task provides the agent with the entire PDF corpus, with all PDFs rendered as images and no machine-readable text available. We observed instances in the trajectories of certain external models where they retrieved reference answers online; Consequently, we assigned a score of zero to these tasks.
Frontier Finance is evaluated with the official finance agent v2 harness.
HANDBOOK.md is evaluated using the official harness built on OpenHands, with evaluation tasks drawn from the benchmark’s early open-source v1 release.
Harvey Legal Agent is evaluated on a public dataset of 1,251 tasks using Artificial Analysis’s Stirrup harness, with performance reported as the all-pass rate (i.e., the percentage of tasks that pass all rubric criteria).
OSWorld V2.1 is evaluated with the Kimi Agent harness in the official OSWorld v2 repo, while GPT-6 Astra's score is taken from Muse Wonder's technical report.
DECK-Arena evaluates presentation generation on real-world queries, while Design Bench covers graphic design via direct and reference-image few-shot prompting; Both run models across python-pptx, pptxjs, and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with integrated search and image generation, using an automated grader calibrated on 10,000+ human judgments.
MCP Atlas. All models are evaluated on the 500-task public subset with a 100-turn limit, using Gemini 3.1 Pro as the judge.
BrowseComp. We adopt the context-compaction strategy used in the Claude model cards, triggered at 200K tokens. We allow a maximum of 500 steps; if this limit is reached before a task is completed, we force the agent to provide an answer, which is then judged. All BrowseComp runs are conducted with temperature=1.0 and top-p=1.0.
GDPval-AA v2.1, AA-Briefcase v1.1 and AutomationBench-AA scores are cited from https://artificialanalysis.ai/ , Apex Agents scores are cited from https://www.mercor.com/apex/apex-agents-leaderboard/
GDP.pdf w/ python, ZeroBench w/ python and ChartoGraphy w/ python are averaged over five runs. Other multimodal benchmarks (w/ python) are averaged over four runs. For GDP.pdf w/ python: Each original PDF file is sent to the sandbox, where the model can use IPython tool to process it. Final responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash (medium reasoning effort) and the official judging prompt. We report the task-macro mean rubric pass rate: for each task, we average the fraction of rubric criteria passed over five independent runs, then average these task-level scores equally across all tasks.
Reasoning & Knowledge & Multimodal benchmarks
GDP.pdf. Each PDF is provided as page images resized to a longest edge of 1,152 pixels, interleaved with Docling-extracted text in page order. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash Medium and the official judging prompt. We report the strict pass rate among fully scored responses.
HLE and HLE-Diamond evaluate general knowledge and reasoning capabilities. We report accuracy on the full evaluation sets, with 2,500 questions for HLE and 1,000 questions for HLE-Diamond. For models marked with an asterisk (*), accuracy is reported on the text-only subset of questions.
GDP.pdf, ZeroBench and ChartoGraphy are averaged over five runs. Other multimodal benchmarks are averaged over four runs. GDP.pdf scores of GLM-5.3 Max and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max is cited from https://artificialanalysis.ai/ .
MMMU-Pro is evaluated following the official protocol, preserving the original input order and prepending images to the text input.
Kimi Hallucination Benchmark evaluates factual accuracy on an internal set of challenging, de-identified prompts drawn from practical work tasks. We report the claim-level hallucination rate assessed by fact-checking agents.
Cybersecurity benchmarks
ExploitBench. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the official ExploitBench harness under the 300-turn budget. We report the pass@5 max capability score: for each environment, the best run across 5 seeds, scored by the number of capability flags reached out of 16, where achieving arbitrary code execution counts as achieving all 16 capabilities. The GPT-6 Astra score is taken from https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ ; the Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.1 scores are taken from https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card ; the GLM-5.3 score is taken from https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3 .
ExploitGym. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the KimiCode harness under a 6-hour wall-clock budget per task. The GPT-6 Astra score is taken from https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ ; the Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.1 scores are taken from https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card at the 6-hour budget; the GLM-5.3 score is taken from https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3 .
xdev-Bench-hard: Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the KimiCode harness. GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 are evaluated with the Claude Code harness.

Oct 23, 2026
OpenAI is closing in on a new funding round of up to $30 billion but has lowered its valuation target to get there. The company originally pitched investors on a $1.4 trillion valuation, according to internal documents obtained by the Financial Times . That number has since dropped to $1.25 trillion, CNBC also reports . The FT says demand was weaker than in previous rounds, with some backers experiencing "indigestion" after heavy investments in earlier fundraises.
UAE investors and investment firm Coatue are leading the $30 billion round. The funding is being positioned as a bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI is also negotiating a commercial deal to secure additional compute capacity through the UAE, according to CNBC.
OpenAI confidentially filed an IPO prospectus with the SEC in June. CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that OpenAI would be a publicly traded company by 2027. CEO Sam Altman said in September that the timing was unfavorable for going public . He had already communicated that internally back in June. Competitor Anthropic is also preparing an IPO and is targeting a valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion. Ad

国务院办公厅：积极增强人工智能创造就业机会等正面效应，有效减缓人工智能应用就业替代影响
2026/10/23 17:17:16 来源： IT之家 作者： 浩渺 责编： 浩渺
评论：
感谢IT之家网友 补药吖 、 西窗 、 有鲫雪狐 的线索投递！
IT之家 10 月 23 日消息，国务院办公厅今日印发《关于适应人工智能技术发展助力构建就业友好型发展方式的意见》。以人工智能赋能高质量发展为契机，以适应技术发展促进高质量充分就业为目标，以构建就业友好型发展方式为方向，积极增强人工智能创造就业机会、赋能传统岗位、提升就业质量、激发创业活力的正面效应， 有效减缓人工智能应用就业替代影响 ，努力实现技术进步、产业升级与就业促进、民生改善相协调的包容性发展。
IT之家注意到，《意见》提出 创造人工智能领域就业创业新模式 。发挥好国家创业投资引导基金、国家人工智能产业投资基金等政府投资基金作用，按照市场化方式支持人工智能领域企业创新发展。建设高水平人工智能开源社区，部署实施一批优质开源项目，形成创业带动就业效应。推行“科技成果＋创业”、“产业发展＋创业”、“职业技能＋创业”、“民生需求＋创业”模式，围绕人工智能应用场景创新、技术成果转化等创业项目，落实创业支持政策，提供创业孵化服务。
加快开发人工智能领域新职业 。围绕人工智能场景培育和大规模应用，加快开发新职业、发布新职业标准，扩大数字化管理师、人工智能工程技术人员、人工智能训练师等新职业新工种需求。鼓励地方结合人工智能产业发展需要，增设相关职称评审专业，及时开展人工智能相关职业技能等级认定。
挖掘传统领域人工智能就业潜能 。发挥人工智能助力传统产业改造升级作用，引导在工业全要素智能化发展和农业数智化转型升级中更好推行人机协作模式，挖掘传统领域数智化就业机会。加快构建人工智能驱动的新型服务方式，分领域推进生产性服务业向专业化和价值链高端延伸，促进生活性服务业高品质、多样化、便利化发展，拓展体验消费、个性消费等服务消费新场景，扩大服务业就业容量。
减缓人工智能应用就业替代影响 。发挥人工智能在改善就业环境、提升职业安全水平、提高工作质效等方面的作用，优先在劳动力紧缺、环境高危等岗位推广应用。稳慎把握人工智能在劳动密集型行业应用的范围、力度、节奏，尽可能减少对从业人员的冲击。鼓励企业探索建立失业缓冲期制度，在大规模推广应用人工智能过程中提前告知受影响劳动者、提供转型转岗就业支持。
加强人工智能应用就业影响研究 。开展人工智能应用就业影响专项调查，持续跟踪人工智能应用渗透、岗位创造替代、技能需求变化等情况。依托高校、科研机构等现有资源，布局一批人工智能就业研究中心。实施好国家社科基金等科研项目，前瞻性研究人工智能技术发展对就业、收入分配的影响。

items.title: Replit 发布 Monitoring Agent，为应用提供可自动修复并部署的值班智能体
items.title_en: Replit Monitoring Agent: Your very own software engineering team
items.summary: Replit 发布 Monitoring Agent，为应用提供相当于自主值班工程师的监控智能体。它可以读取生产日志和指标调查错误、变慢和部署失败，在启用 autofix 后验证修复并邮件汇报，启用 auto-publish 后可自动部署修复。该能力建立在早前上线的 App Monitoring 之上，用户可在应用的 Publishing 设置中开启。

Replit Monitoring Agent: Your very own software engineering team
Replit Monitoring Agent can detect production issues, investigate the cause, validate a fix, and publish it automatically.
Published:
Oct 22, 2026
Akram Hussein
Carl Cortright
Anyone who has published an app knows that dreaded message from a user: “Doesn’t work for me”.
At a large company, an on-call engineer gets paged, investigates the problem, and works to get the app running again. For most creators and small teams, that responsibility falls to the same person building the product, supporting customers, and trying to grow the business.
Today, we’re changing that.
Replit Monitoring Agent gives every internal app builder and entrepreneur an autonomous on-call engineer for their app.
When a production issue occurs, the Monitoring Agent can investigate the alert, identify the cause, make and validate a fix, and deploy that fix to production. It then reports back with what happened and what changed.
Earlier this year, we launched App Monitoring , giving you production health checks and alerts when a published app went down. Now, we’re closing the loop. When you run apps on Replit, your agent doesn’t just tell you what broke, it makes the fix as well.
Now, instead of learning about outages from frustrated users, you can wake up and focus on what matters to you, with the peace of mind that your app’s uptime is being handled.
How Monitoring Agent Works
Once your app is in production, keeping it running means understanding what’s happening, responding when something breaks, and safely shipping a fix.
Replit Monitoring Agent is a first-of-its-kind agent that can see, fix, and deploy changes autonomously for AI-app creators.
See what is happening in production
Agent can access your production logs and metrics, giving it the context to investigate errors, slowdowns, and failed deployments without you digging through logs.
Fix issues before users report them
With alerting and autofix enabled, Monitoring Agent is notified when an issue occurs. It investigates the cause, validates a fix, and emails you a summary of what happened.
Deploy fixes automatically
With auto-publish enabled, Monitoring Agent can deploy a validated fix and report back with what changed. You decide whether fixes are published automatically.
Toward Autonomous Software Teams
Replit was the first platform to enable agentic coding in the cloud. As agents become more capable, our focus is expanding from a single coding agent to autonomous software teams that can accomplish anything a modern software engineering team can do, and more.
We believe the future of software is teams of agents working together to build, maintain, secure, and optimize software, while creators set the direction and stay in control.
Over the past six months, we’ve launched industry-leading systems for black box security scanning , growth , and now production monitoring. These are important steps toward autonomous agent teams that can manage any app, tool, or business built on Replit.
All of this is in service of a simple idea: more people should be able to turn their ideas into something real. Building an app is only one part of that journey. Keeping it reliable, secure, discoverable, and improving over time has historically required an entire team. By giving every creator access to agents that can do that work, more people can create, launch, and grow software without needing to become experts in every discipline.
All you need is the idea and the ambition.
Get Started
Publish your app, open its Publishing settings, and enable monitoring alerts and auto-fix.
You can also turn on auto-publish to allow Monitoring Agent to deploy validated fixes automatically.
Your app is live. Now its on-call engineer can be, too.
For more information, see our documentation .
More
Sep 10, 2026 Databricks Integration is Now Available with Native Lakebase Support
The Replit | Databricks integration gives enterprise teams a faster path to utilizing governed data for production-ready applications. Today, we’re excited to announce the integration is generally available alongside a new capability: native Databricks Lakebase support. This builds on the foundation introduced from our public preview announcement this past June.
The result is one seamless path from idea to production: Replit accelerates application creation, while Databricks hosts and provides governed access and security to live enterprise data. Through Lakebase, Databricks also delivers a managed database for storing and updating application data.
With native Lakebase support, teams can build full-stack, context-rich apps that combine live Databricks warehouse data with information created and updated through the app. When an app built with Replit is ready to deploy, Replit Agent automatically provisions its Lakebase database, eliminating the need for manual setup.
New Capabilities for a Faster, Safer Launch
Automated Preview Deploys: Test your apps before they go live. Replit automatically creates a separate preview environment that keeps test data isolated from live business data in Databricks, giving teams a safe place to build, review changes, and make adjustments.
Jul 29, 2026 Introducing Replit Design
The next era of design, for everyone
Jun 17, 2026 Replit is now available in Claude
Replit is now available directly inside Claude, making it easier than ever to go from a conversation to a fully built, shipped product - without losing context, in one seamless workflow.
Design in Claude, Build in Replit
You can now design on-brand, beautiful apps in Claude Design using natural language. Once your design is ready, send it directly to Replit to continue building, refining, and shipping your app—all through natural language and in one seamless workflow.
No copy-pasting, no context switching, no friction.

Elizabeth Lopatto
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.
Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips , but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on , which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently , but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered .) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft . At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement
SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Macrohard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership , but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028 . He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.
The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger
Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.
Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.
Basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money
Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine , a longtime Musk observer . But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”
Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.
Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted . “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.
From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:
It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.
It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?
The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax . Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing , and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing , and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “ there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”
Shares and shares alike
Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”
At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”
If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more for Tesla, Musk gets a payout
Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone.
Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS , so it’s not impossible.
What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth , according to Bloomberg . More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package . If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away.

THE HUMANIST REVIEW OF AI
THE HUMANIST REVIEW OF AI

Health
Building Medical Superintelligence
MAI Health Team October 22, 2026 Health
MAI Health Team LI
X
FB
What if AI could help clinicians work through a complex medical diagnosis, step by step, and achieve higher accuracy, at lower cost, with fewer medical tests?
That future is now coming into view. On common presentations to a US emergency department, MAI-DxO – our AI diagnostic system – is 1.7 times more accurate than physicians when evaluated using cases from MIMIC-IV-ED.
And on medicine’s most complex cases, published in The New England Journal of Medicine , MAI-DxO is more than twice as accurate as physicians using textbooks and the internet – and nearly four times as accurate when they diagnose without those resources. It also manages to do this at half or even one third of the cost, getting to the right diagnosis with fewer tests and procedures.
Our work is published today in Science .
Read more about our vision for medical superintelligence also published this week in BMJ Digital Health and AI .

Rethinking How AI is Built and Tested
AI has the potential to transform health and healthcare, and progress is accelerating rapidly. The challenge now is to build and rigorously evaluate AI systems that translate advances in their clinical reasoning capabilities into meaningful impact.
Today’s paper, building on earlier work , i ntroduces two foundations for that shift: the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark (SDBench), which tests step-by-step diagnostic reasoning, and the Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), our leading AI system on the benchmark.
Medical licensing exams such as the United States Medical Licensing Exams (USMLEs) are designed to assess physicians’ knowledge – not the realities of making a clinical diagnosis. In these tests, all information is presented upfront and a single answer is selected; in practice, clinicians must build the picture step by step, deciding what to ask, which tests to order and how each new finding changes the likely diagnosis. Such exams have become the common benchmarks for evaluating the performance of health AI .
That’s why we developed SDBench, which evaluates performance across two complementary sets of cases: 304 complex cases taken from The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) case proceedings and a set of more typical emergency-department presentations from MIMIC-IV-ED. Each becomes an interactive case in which AI models and/or physicians start with limited information and choose what to request next. The benchmark measures diagnostic accuracy, evidence requested and estimated test costs – assessing both the answer and the path taken.
We built MAI-DxO and tested it within SDBench. Rather than relying on one model for an immediate answer, it operates like a panel of virtual physicians: each proposing diagnoses, selecting useful questions or tests, and challenging the emerging view. MAI-DxO coordinates this exchange over several rounds of debate, updating its assessment as evidence arrives and weighing each test’s likely value against its cost.
What we found:
On complex NEJM cases, MAI-DxO achieved 83% diagnostic accuracy. Physicians achieved 22% without external reference resources and 36% with them, making MAI-DxO about 3.7 and 2.3 times more accurate, respectively.
On more typical emergency-department cases from MIMIC-IV-ED, MAI-DxO achieved 80% accuracy versus 47% for physicians – more than 1.7 times higher.
When optimised more heavily for cost, MAI-DxO performance remained strong while choosing more cost-effective workups. On NEJM cases, one configuration achieved 81% accuracy at less than half the cost of comparative systems.
Across both datasets, no other human or AI approach was both more accurate and less costly than MAI-DxO.
These gains persisted – and improved – when we repeated the evaluation with newer models, including GPT-5.5, without changing the orchestration method, suggesting the approach is not tied to one model generation.
We are open-sourcing SDBench for select NEJM cases – including the benchmark, Gatekeeper, Judge and cost-estimation code – so researchers can reproduce the evaluation, test other models, and challenge or extend the findings.
Explore SDBench


From Better Diagnosis to Better Care
Diagnosis is only one part of the care journey. Better care also requires keeping pace with medical knowledge, selecting the right treatment, understanding change over time, and supporting choices that reflect a person’s values and access to care. The opportunity is to unite these capabilities into a standard of care not widely available today. In The Building Blocks of Medical Superintelligence , published in BMJ Digital Health and AI , we explore what it would take for AI to support this broader vision – and ultimately exceed the capabilities of today’s strongest clinical teams and health systems.
Sequential diagnosis offers an early example: AI physicians collaborating, challenging assumptions and refining their clinical reasoning as evidence emerges. Our ambition is to build AI that connects knowledge, context and decisions across the care journey – not simply excels at one clinical task. Through our collaboration with Mayo Clinic , we aim to combine frontier AI, clinical expertise and longitudinal multimodal data to build systems for the complexity and diversity of real-world care.
Testing in the Real World
Benchmarks matter, but the true test is performance in real clinical environments. Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, we will evaluate clinical reasoning capabilities across different hospital settings. In a prospective study, patients will interact with the system directly, with performance measured against physicians’ independent assessments. Working alongside clinical teams will show where the technology succeeds, where it falls short and how it can fit into busy workflows.
Health at Microsoft
Rapid advances in medical AI are opening new possibilities for patients and clinicians. To turn this progress into practical impact, we are bringing together health teams from across Microsoft – including scientists from Microsoft Research and the teams behind products like Dragon Copilot and PowerScribe – into an integrated effort at Microsoft AI. Working together, we will accelerate the delivery of trusted AI systems that drive better clinical outcomes and care experiences.
Build the Future With Us
We’re a lean, fast-moving lab made up of some of the world’s most talented minds. We have an exciting roadmap of compute at MAI, which is ramping quickly and extensively. And we have an ambitious mission we truly believe in. We’re also fortunate to partner with incredible product teams giving our models the chance to reach billions of users and create immense positive impact. If you’re a brilliant, highly-ambitious and low ego individual, you’ll fit right in—come and join us as we work on our next generation of models!

items.title: Anthropic 分析 Claude Mythos 5 在 UK AISI CTF 测试中的对齐失当行为
items.title_en: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident

An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Chapter 01 : Alignment assessment summary
Published
Oct 23, 2026
Team
Alignment
Topics
Alignment
Cybersecurity
Safety evaluations
