← AI News AI News OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program is 1 of 2 parties to discover PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in core PHP affecting 70% of the web, using GPT-5.6 Sol; coordinated response over 2 months
The Big Hardening begins
Latent Space Oct 22 · 37 min read
Share
Almost 2 months ago, OpenAI introduced Daybreak for Frontline Defenders , a $1B subsidy for access to Daybreak cyber models and products. That funding came into use almost immediately, as major vulnerabilities in PHP were independently discovered by two parties: Ryan Austin, a researcher at the security firm Calif, as part of the OpenAI “ Patch the Planet ” project in August 2026 using GPT 5.6 Sol:
View post on X
… as well as Wiz, recently acquired into Google Cloud (using Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas).
All high profile cyber disclosures are at least a little bit of marketing, and the degree to which this was a severely alarming vulnerability on the order of famous ones like log4shell and Heartbleed is up to some debate , but surely the coordinated response across the PHP Ecosystem is the developer community responding in its most ideal form.
We should expect to be in for at least a year of finding such critical vulnerabilities; but it is the wrong move to blame the messenger for finding them; rather it is good to know that our critical software is generally getting the biggest security audit it has ever had in human history.
AI News for 10/20/2026-10/21/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies!
AI Twitter Recap
Top Story: PHP2Shell—chronology, core claims, and the complications behind the emergency response
What happened
Researchers disclosed two PHP-engine memory-corruption vulnerabilities, with demonstrated unauthenticated exploitation against major CMSs and an unusually broad coordinated response.
The researchers named the vulnerabilities PHP2Shell and identified them as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Their technical description places the defects in PHP’s internal handling of out-of-memory conditions and fatal errors—not in a WordPress plugin or an application’s authentication logic. They report demonstrations of full remote code execution and “Heartbleed-style” memory disclosure. @sagitz_
The disclosed demonstrations included pre-authentication RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. The researcher’s announcement separately claims remote memory disclosure against any PHP application. These are researcher-reported exploit results; they should not be silently expanded into a claim that every deployment has an identical, immediately exploitable RCE path. @sagitz_
OpenAI says Calif researchers used its models to discover the flaws, while secondary reporting says Wiz independently found the same bugs. Posts identify GPT-5.6 Sol on the Calif/OpenAI side; a Wiz-affiliated account credits Gemini 4 Argon with discovery, exploit-chain development, detector creation, and patch validation. This is a multi-party discovery story, not evidence that one vendor alone found and fixed the issue. @TheRundownAI , @steipete , @ralucaadapopa
OpenAI describes approximately two months of coordinated remediation before disclosure. It says the patch required a major PHP-engine change and coordination among maintainers, researchers, security providers, and governments. A participating researcher confirms work with the PHP Foundation to support and harden the patch. @OpenAI , @itszn13
Cloudflare deployed initial WAF mitigations before the scheduled patch release. Its CTO said rules covered known exploit vectors, were available to all customers including the free tier, and were being updated as early attacks emerged. He explicitly called the rules a stopgap and directed operators to patch at 14:00 UTC . @dok2001
The supplied NSA account advised preparation for an immediate update—and taking systems offline if timely mitigation was not possible. Later OpenAI messaging said upgrades were available; secondary reporting says details leaked before the patch. The supplied material does not establish precisely what leaked, when, or whether the release schedule changed. @NSACyber , @OpenAI , @TheRundownAI
Reconstructing the chronology
1. Discovery and private coordination: approximately two months before public disclosure. OpenAI places the work under Patch the Planet and says it led a coalition preparing fixes and protections. Its security researcher Eric Wallace adds that internal teams worked on patching and detection rather than merely disclosing the bug, with confidential advance notification to governments and outside agencies. Greg Brockman reiterates the two-month coordination period. These are participant accounts, not an independently audited incident timeline. @Eric_Wallace_ , @gdb
The distinction between program names matters: the posts associate the vulnerability with Patch the Planet , while researchers credit Daybreak model access for enabling security work. Those are related roles—remediation initiative versus access mechanism—not interchangeable descriptions of the same program. @OpenAI , @S1r1u5_
2. Advance public warnings and a scheduled patch window. Japanese-language posts warned operators to prepare for a 23:00 JST, October 21 release, consistent with Cloudflare’s 14:00 UTC announcement. One correctly emphasized that a PHP-core vulnerability cannot be fixed merely by waiting for plugin developers. Another framed the event as a “15-minute” race after patch publication, but that number was a prediction—not a measured time to weaponization. @ds_nakajima , @expokun
3. Pre-release filtering and observed attack activity. Cloudflare’s post is the strongest firsthand operational evidence in the supplied record: mitigations were already deployed, known vectors were covered, and “early attacks” were appearing. It does not specify successful compromises, request counts, victim counts, payload provenance, or whether the traffic represented original exploit development versus reuse of leaked information. @dok2001
4. Research disclosure, government warning, and patch availability. The researcher’s public thread describes the exploit demonstrations and error-handling root cause. The NSA post calls for urgent preparation and conditional shutdown. OpenAI subsequently says every PHP site can upgrade safely. The supplied set contains no direct PHP Foundation release advisory, exact fixed-version matrix, distribution package identifiers, or patch commit. That missing primary-source layer prevents a reliable “upgrade to version X” instruction. @sagitz_ , @NSACyber , @OpenAI
5. Alleged premature exposure and widespread service disruption. The Rundown reports that details leaked early. A later viral compilation adds approximately 1.5 million servers , attributed to Censys, running versions without a fix; reported shutdowns involving Dutch institutions, government sites elsewhere in Europe, Wikipedia, Archive.org, Asana, GOG, and others; and a 05:55 warning from Japan’s prime minister. None of those individual claims is corroborated by its underlying advisory, measurement, or status page in the supplied material. Nor does the record establish whether each outage was a precaution, a patching interruption, an unrelated failure, or a compromise. @TheRundownAI , @fiveoutofnine
SemiAnalysis separately reports that Japan’s prime minister urged PHP operators to patch immediately or temporarily disconnect if they could not. Its account contextualizes that response with an existing Japanese breach wave, rather than establishing that PHP2Shell caused those earlier incidents. @SemiAnalysis_
6. Exposure-checking assistance followed disclosure. OpenAI published a repository containing a Codex skill intended to guide operators through checking whether their sites were affected. That is an assistance workflow, not a substitute for a vendor advisory, package verification, or evidence that every vulnerable runtime has been replaced. @OpenAI
AI’s role: credible evidence, competing credit, and unresolved causality
The affirmative case is stronger than a benchmark-only claim. Researchers describe working exploit chains, coordinated patch engineering, detectors, and patch validation. A participating researcher calls PHP2Shell the most consequential vulnerability they have helped discover. OpenAI characterizes it as an example of the “Defender’s Window” : advanced models finding a flaw before attackers, giving defenders time to prepare. Importantly, its wording is “to our knowledge” —not proof that no attacker previously knew the vulnerabilities. @itszn13 , @OpenAI
Credit is distributed across humans, models, and infrastructure providers. Calif/OpenAI and Wiz/Gemini appear as separate discovery accounts; PHP maintainers supplied the upstream remediation path; Cloudflare supplied pre-release filtering. Google also advertises Wiz testing in which Gemini 4 Argon found more than twice as many vulnerabilities as baseline models , but the supplied promotional post does not expose the dataset, baselines, budgets, or false-positive accounting. It is not an independent comparative evaluation of PHP2Shell discovery performance. @TheRundownAI , @ralucaadapopa , @Google
Researcher-access policy draws both praise and criticism. One researcher credits OpenAI’s Daybreak access with a portfolio of findings spanning PHP, GitLab, Chrome, WordPress, and other targets. Another sharply contrasts OpenAI’s vetted access with Anthropic’s restrictions; the claim that Anthropic contributed “zero value” is that author’s sweeping opinion, not established by the PHP record. A further post criticizes restrictions on Astra access and argues for giving 1,000 vetted researchers the best available models with intensive monitoring, rather than a rigid red/blue distinction. @S1r1u5_ , @migtissera , @S1r1u5_
The countervailing safety rationale appears in reporting that Anthropic delayed broad access to Mythos-class models for four months to strengthen cyber safeguards. That provides context for restricted access, but does not settle whether its implementation helped or hindered this particular remediation effort. @kimmonismus
A burst of disclosures is not, by itself, evidence of a burst of AI-caused compromises. The supplied feed mixes defensive discovery, supply-chain attacks, credential theft, precautionary shutdowns, and unrelated vulnerabilities. Ethan Mollick interprets the moment as attack and defense accelerating beyond human response speeds; John Allard describes a capability “phase transition” while acknowledging that many recent findings came from white-hat programs. Both are interpretations of the pattern, not incident-level causal attribution. @emollick , @john__allard
Operational complications: patching, shutdowns, and the temptation to “fix everything”
The emergency is as much distribution and ownership as discovery. Operators need to locate PHP across managed hosting, containers, appliances, background workers, and old applications; obtain appropriate packages; deploy them; restart or replace affected processes; and verify the running build. One operator describes maintaining numerous PHP/WordPress sites and being exhausted by testing and updates. Another concludes that patch distribution is poorly coordinated. @ostrisai , @jd_pressman
WAF deployment reduces immediate exposure but creates a false-confidence risk. Cloudflare’s own statement is narrower than the later advice to put all internet-facing services behind it: known vectors were covered, protections were evolving, and patching remained mandatory. Proxied coverage, alternate ingress paths, and the origin’s exposure must be checked rather than assumed. @dok2001 , @threepointone
Shutdown guidance is conditional, not evidence that the entire internet should disconnect. The supplied NSA post recommends taking systems offline when immediate updating is infeasible until full mitigation is possible. For a specific operator, the relevant questions are affected-version status, exposure, available mitigations, and the consequences of continued operation—not the engagement score of an alarming post. @NSACyber
“Use the RCE to auto-patch every server” is a proposal, not an authorized remediation plan. Marc Köhlbrugge raises the idea; J. D. Pressman suggests a presidential pardon for a lab or white-hat team attempting it. Unsolicited exploitation still risks unauthorized access, outages, incorrect fixes, destruction of evidence, and cross-jurisdictional liability. A speculative pardon does not provide universal authorization or eliminate civil and foreign legal exposure. @marckohlbrugge , @jd_pressman
Update velocity has a supply-chain trade-off. One widely shared post captures the dilemma: updating constantly can expose users to compromised packages, while delaying updates leaves known vulnerabilities open. Pressman argues that endless patching is unsustainable unless the rate of new vulnerabilities and risky releases falls; he also notes that receiving no patch and discovering theft is worse than receiving too many updates. @xeophon , @jd_pressman , @jd_pressman
The longer-term alternatives remain open questions. Sarah Guo reports CVEs increasing from roughly 4,000 per month to 15,000 since April , and asks about formal verification, safer distributions, and organizations without red teams. The counts are not independently verified here, and disclosure volume is not a direct measure of successful exploitation. Other posts ask what a full-codebase security sweep would cost and recast the challenge as hardening mundane infrastructure rather than debating only abstract catastrophe. @saranormous , @saranormous , @teortaxesTex , @mimi10v3
For an incident team, the defensible sequence is to obtain the authoritative PHP and distribution advisories, inventory exposed runtimes, apply temporary protections where justified, deploy authenticated fixed packages, verify running processes, and investigate evidence of exploitation separately. Updating closes a vulnerability; it does not establish that credentials or data were never exposed.
Public reactions: practical caution versus unsupported escalation
The precautionary perspective stresses that interconnected services are fragile and remediation can be costly. Joshua Achiam compares the moment to March 2020 , speculates about internet lockdowns, recommends backing up valued internet material, and suggests printing important records. Pressman says remediation costs exceeded his expectations. These are preparedness judgments—not evidence of impending systemic collapse. Paper copies may help continuity but are not inherently tamperproof logs. @jachiam0 , @jachiam0 , @jachiam0 , @jd_pressman
The alarm-skeptical perspective asks for specificity. Alex Johnson argues that warnings about bank accounts being arbitrarily emptied obscure the distinction between unauthorized transfers and scams in which customers authorize payment. He invokes U.S. Electronic Funds Transfer Act protections with timely reporting; those protections are jurisdiction-, account-, and circumstance-dependent, not a universal guarantee. Kelsey Piper separately warns about the psychological cost of living under constant annihilation framing. @AlexH_Johnson , @KelseyTuoc
Broad personal-security advice needs to be separated from the PHP fix. Password managers, unique credentials, strong MFA, patching, carrier port-out protections, and U.S.-specific credit or tax identity safeguards can reduce downstream harm. But enabling 2FA does not prevent exploitation of an unauthenticated PHP-engine bug. Likewise, viral advice to avoid all online payments the next day is not supported by a demonstrated scope assessment. @peterwildeford , @StillMare_
The broader threat context is real but not interchangeable with PHP2Shell. SemiAnalysis reports 18 Japanese companies disclosing breaches since September 25, including exposures of approximately 6.6 million Times Car accounts , 11.18 million Burger King Japan app records , and potentially 22.5 million Sourcenext records . It attributes findings about AI-assisted scanning and API attacks to JPCERT/CC. Another post quotes an August 19 advisory concerning AI-assisted tooling against internet-exposed Siemens PLCs. These are separate reported incidents and advisories; neither establishes PHP2Shell as their entry point. @SemiAnalysis_ , @AndrewCurran_
The key unresolved evidence gaps are concrete: exact affected and fixed versions; CVSS vectors; deployment prerequisites; the independent discovery timeline; what leaked before release; successful exploitation versus scanning; validated exposure counts; and the cause and duration of each reported shutdown. The supplied viral incident compilation cannot answer those questions merely by placing PHP, GitLab, LiteLLM, Railway, certificate-authority failures, and government warnings in the same narrative. @fiveoutofnine
Other News
Flint and Automated Research: Local Coding Models, Smaller Teams and Scientific Workflows
Flint launches with broad local-serving support : Recursive released an Apache-2.0 coding MoE with roughly 40B total parameters, 2.5B active parameters and a 262K-token context window. LM Studio says it requires approximately 24GB locally. Recursive positions it as an on-device complement to—not a replacement for—frontier cloud agents ( launch , specifications ).
Claimed results : Recursive reports 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89.7% on SWE-bench Pro v2 and 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified. These are release claims, not independent replication ( results ).
Performance : Advertised short-context speeds exceed 125 tokens/s on a MacBook Pro and 150 tokens/s on RTX Spark. A separate user measured 114–132 output tokens/s on an M5 Max with int4 MLX; that is useful corroboration of speed, not a controlled capability evaluation ( local measurement ).
Research contribution : Recursive says its Eureka Machine participated across ideation, implementation and validation, contributing sparse architecture choices, low-bit training and kernels. It claims a 71% size reduction with almost no quality loss and development from scratch in under four months ( method ).
Availability : Day-zero integrations span local frameworks and hosted access. vLLM reports 500 tokens/s on one GB200 at 100K context using NVFP4 without speculative decoding; OpenRouter offers free launch access ( vLLM , OpenRouter ).
Mirendil claims one-researcher pretraining at scale : Mirendil says its first base model was built by one researcher in 3.5 months for less than $10M in compute, including research experiments and the final run. It discloses unusually broad parameter ranges—100B–500B for Base, 500B–2T for Large and 2T–10T for XL—rather than precise configurations. Independent evaluations, post-training results and API access are still forthcoming, so this is a consequential efficiency claim awaiting external validation ( announcement ).
JOLT jointly trains the teacher and student : Perplexity and NVIDIA’s post-training work addresses a weakness in self-distillation: a privileged teacher can exploit shortcuts unavailable to its student. JOLT trains the teacher using outcome rewards while penalizing excessive divergence from the student. The authors report matching GRPO on MATH with 6.5× fewer training tokens; JOLT+, which adds student outcome rewards, beats GRPO across five evaluated benchmarks ( method and results , benchmark summary ).
GPT-Rosalind generates testable biological hypotheses : OpenAI reports thousands of agents linking gene-expression results from millions of mouse-brain cells with literature in 32 minutes. One proposed mechanism connects DCTN1 disruption to impaired cholesterol transport; another examines differences between TSC1 and TSC2 disruption in cerebellar neurons. These are hypotheses for experimental follow-up—not demonstrated treatments or validated drug targets ( DCTN1 work , TSC2 follow-up ).
Inference Systems: DeepInfer Economics, Native TPU Support and Power-Aware Capacity
DeepInfer exposes production scheduling techniques : DeepSeek’s released framework combines speculative decoding, dynamic prefill sizing, decode balancing by request count and KV length, and overlapping CPU scheduling with GPU execution. A particularly reusable idea is adjusting speculative verification length using predicted draft acceptance and measured hardware throughput, making batches more regular instead of allowing slow replicas to determine completion time ( technical analysis ).
Cache accounting : A deployment-report summary cites 1.5M input tokens/s per prefill accelerator including cache hits , versus 60K excluding hits at a 96% cache-hit rate; decode is reported at 14K output tokens/s per accelerator. These are materially different throughput quantities ( report summary ).
Economics caveat : The same summary describes approximately $38 per accelerator-hour as revenue , not profit. Server, electricity, cooling and staffing costs remain outside that figure.
Independent benchmarking remains contested : SemiAnalysis says DeepInfer is absent from InferenceX because essential serving components are missing and reconstructing them would require too many assumptions. Its subsequent profitability comparison drew criticism for mixing hardware generations, peak versus off-peak prices, and revenue versus profit. The criticism is itself an attributed analysis, not a settled replication result; the practical requirement is matched hardware, workload, cache assumptions, SLOs and pricing before comparing economics ( benchmark limitation , comparison critique ).
TorchTPU opens a native PyTorch path : Google open-sourced TorchTPU for training and serving through familiar PyTorch tooling. SGLang’s plugin is reportedly powering production inference at Meta and supports several current open models; its custom MegaKernel reaches a claimed 770 decode tokens/s for Muse Spark Open at batch size one on an 8K-input/1K-output workload. vLLM-TorchTPU adds prefix caching, speculative decoding and disaggregated serving ( Google , SGLang , vLLM ).
GTC emphasizes deployment speed and power utilization : NVIDIA’s DSX POD packages AI infrastructure into containerized building blocks, with coverage claiming capacity expansion in days rather than months. More concretely, Lambda demonstrated 19 HGX B200 nodes operating within the power budget of 16 using DSX MaxLPS. Treat deployment timelines as product claims and the node result as a proof of concept, not fleet-wide capacity already delivered ( DSX POD , Lambda demonstration ).
Evaluation Integrity and Agent Engineering: Measure the Harness, Not Just the Model
Medical reasoning exposes completeness–accuracy tradeoffs : Artificial Analysis revised MLCR-AA’s prompts, reference answers and three-model judging panel. Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra tie at 41.7%, with no model exceeding 42% under the combined completeness-and-accuracy requirement. Claude leads completeness; OpenAI leads record-grounded accuracy. Revised scores are not directly comparable with the previous methodology ( results , methodology ).
Length confound : A cross-benchmark analysis finds Claude answers approximately 4–6× longer than OpenAI’s; each added claim creates another opportunity to contradict the record. Raw rubric scores, completeness and length-adjusted quality therefore produce different rankings ( comparison ).
SWE-bench Multimodal faces an ablation challenge : An independent investigation argues that v2 does not meaningfully require images; a separate researcher highlights running the benchmark without images as the essential sanity check. This is a substantive critique of what the benchmark measures, not proof that its underlying coding tasks lack value ( investigation , ablation discussion ).
Evolved harnesses and interfaces improve fixed executors : Two papers strengthen the case for optimizing the environment around agents.
OO-Harness : Specialized subclasses, execution-derived design lessons and routing raise AutomationBench from 61.6% to 77.4% with the same Gemini 3.5 Flash executor; Workspace-Bench rises from 25.5% to 39.5% ( paper summary ).

items.summary: NSA 警告两个由 Calif 研究人员用 GPT-5.6 Sol 发现的 PHP 关键漏洞（PHP2Shell），敦促组织打补丁或将未修补服务器下线。两个漏洞位于 PHP 核心，在 Apache mod_php 上演示的利用可在应用代码运行前触发。

X 上的 Rohan Paul：“National Security Agency (NSA) and world leaders warn of security flaws found in PHP programming language
Calif researchers first found this flaw using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol
In Europe, Asia and on other continents, authorities have taken a number of government websites offline for the time being to protect them from newly identified security vulnerabilities in a programming language that powers the vast majority of websites online.
The NSA told organizations to patch 2 critical PHP flaws, dubbed PHP2Shell, or pull unpatched servers offline.
Both bugs live in PHP’s core, so every installation serving web requests is at risk, whatever site runs on top.
When a request exhausts memory or hits a fatal error, PHP can leave half-built or freed memory that cleanup code or later requests trust.
On Apache’s mod_php, a demonstrated exploit triggers the corruption before any application code runs, so logins and app-level checks cannot block it.
Cloudflare saw attacks before PHP shipped fixed versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 on October 21.
VirusTotal counts about 5.1M IP addresses running PHP, and about 758K that show a version run end-of-life branches with no patched release.
That long tail will set how long PHP2Shell stays exploitable, since each owner must upgrade, find a backport or take the server offline.”

items.title: AI 挖出潜伏十几年的 PHP 底层漏洞，PHP2Shell 事件全景复盘
items.title_en: AI挖出藏了十几年的底层PHP漏洞，网络安全也回不去那个旧时代了。
items.summary: 作者复盘 PHP2Shell 事件：两个 CVSS 满分定为 9.2 分的 PHP 远程代码执行漏洞（CVE-2026-109618 和 CVE-2026-109619）在补丁发布前泄露，攻击演示视频外流，多国政府网站预防性下线，OpenAI 认领漏洞由 GPT-5.6 Sol 辅助发现。
items.fullContent:
X 上的 数字生命卡兹克：“https://t.co/GemeEkhQGx” / X
文章
登录 注册
文章
登录 注册
数字生命卡兹克
@Khazix0918
AI挖出藏了十几年的底层PHP漏洞，网络安全也回不去那个旧时代了。
13 分钟阅读
昨晚，可能是网络安全的噩梦。
也是很多工程师的，不眠之夜。
只能说，我们整个时代和社会，在AI的加速下，都会变得焦头烂额中。
事情是这样的。
首先是前天，也就是10月20日夜里11点多，Hacker News上突然冒出来一条帖子。
标题巨吓人，说是两个CVSS 10.0的PHP远程代码执行漏洞，即将公开。
发帖的人自己写着，除了“信源：信我就行”（trust me, bro）之外，我没有任何证据，然后甚至还附上了漏洞编号。
不过呢，这种帖子，网上一天能刷到一百条，没人当真。
但这一条，几个小时后被一家叫watchTowr的安全公司确认了。他们的原话是：“我们本来都该等到周四的。”
这一下就尴尬了，因为这个漏洞是巨大的，已经处于泄密状态了，真的有心人已经可以开始利用，但PHP官方的安全更新还在打包中，原定于22号晚上更新，可这瞬间就有两天的空档，如果这两天之内漏洞被利用且被攻破，后果不堪设想。
又过了一个多小时，PHP官方急忙发了预告：原定10月22日的安全更新，被迫提前到21日晚上10点（北京时间），尽可能的压缩时间。
结果，官方预告刚发出去，又出了个更离谱的事。
一家参与发现这两个漏洞的安全公司，叫Calif，居然不小心把一段攻击演示视频发到了网上，充分的说明了，这个世界就是一个巨大的草台班子。
视频里，他们展示了如何利用这些漏洞，在多个目标上成功运行攻击验证程序，虽然视频很快就删了，但没办法，手快已经有人保存下来，开始在社区上大肆传播。
这下好了。
原本大家只知道有两个严重漏洞，连具体怎么攻击都不知道，现在，连攻击演示视频都有了，就差手把手教学了。
然后在各种离谱的AI加速之下，安全研究人员开始加速复现，网上各种号称能利用漏洞的代码也开始冒出来。
而这时候，距离可以修复安全漏洞的补丁推出给所有人可被正式下载，还有，16个小时。
生死时速的16个小时，如果是以前，恶意之人，可能还没办法在这么短的时间里发起大规模的攻击，但是如今，是AI时代了，16个小时，对于用AI加速后的人们来说，好像有点太长了。
更离谱的是，21日下午3点41分，一家做容器镜像的公司，比约定时间提前了6个多小时，把已经打好补丁的镜像发了出去，PHP基金会直接开骂了：“无视了多方数周的协调工作。”
因为这年头，懂行的人拿新旧两版代码让AI直接暴力对比一下，直接就知道漏洞在哪了，用AI研究补丁，用AI逆向分析漏洞，再用AI开发攻击程序。
但大量正常网站的管理员，却还没有能够直接安装的更新包，这意味着攻击者直接开了天眼，直接抢跑。
于是，崩溃发生了。
21日这一天，荷兰的数字身份系统、议会网站，连国家网络安全中心自己的网站，挨个下线。
芬兰政府的IT服务商也关掉了一批服务，美国一家做人力资源软件的公司 BambooHR直接停服，提醒客户发薪相关业务可能受到影响，日本的 niconico和pixiv进入紧急维护。
因为日本的PHP网站实在太多了，甚至高市早苗都去X上发文，建议预防性下线，直到晚上10点的PHP更新推送。
一个编程语言的漏洞，让高市早苗半夜发推，让好几个国家的政府主动拔网线，这种画面，说实话，我真没见过。
就这样，世界跌跌撞撞，撑过了这十几个小时。
无人知道，在这十几个小时中，水下的黑暗面里，获得了什么。
晚上10点，PHP安全更新上线，对于这两项严重漏洞来说，没有任何完整的缓解措施，更新是唯一安全的选择。
同时，OpenAI出来认领，PHP这两个史诗级的安全漏洞，是GPT辅助发现的。
而这个漏洞，还不是啥新模型整的，是几个月前，用GPT-5.6 Sol发现的，所以大家就可以想象，如果是这些大模型公司的未发布的内部的更强模型去扫的话，全世界的各种网络基建，那可能真的全都有问题。。。
同时，OpenAI这次也紧急发布了一个skill，来辅助你发现，你的网站是否会受到影响。
这里希望大家一定要注意，如果你自己的网站中，使用了PHP，如果你还不知道这些消息，请看到的第一时间，立刻，立刻更新版本，也希望能扩散给你的朋友。
我知道，很多人会说，不就是一个漏洞吗？有什么大惊小怪的。
那我觉得，要理解这次为什么闹这么大，全球反应为啥这么过度，得先知道PHP是个什么东西。
我也不是啥专家，我只能用我知道的语言，尽力描述一下。
首先，我们可能都知道，你在浏览器里点开一个网页，服务器那边得现场算出来这一页该显示什么，比如你是谁，购物车里有什么，这篇文章下面有几条评论等等，那干这个活的程序，叫后端。
而PHP，就是写后端最常用的语言之一。
不过因为太老了，现在很多公司的新产品或者新技术栈都不太用了，并且有意思的是，PHP在程序员圈子里一直是被嘲的对象，“PHP是世界上最好的语言”，当了十几年的梗，很多人都觉得它是上个世纪的东西。
但在全球，用PHP搭的网站，依然占据着70%，即使是新一点的国内，虽然Java极多，以2026年10月的数据看，依然还有超过一半的网站，是用PHP搭的。
人人都嘲它，但说实话，也人人都离不开它。
你注册过的论坛、小店的付款页、很多地方政府的办事网站、公司内部的报销系统，还有路由器和NAS的管理后台，大概率都有一个跑在PHP上的。
它就像城市地下的老水管，平时确实没人想起它，一旦爆了，整条街都能喷的全是屎。
而这一次，就是PHP本身爆掉了。
这次的漏洞有个名字，叫PHP2Shell。Shell就是服务器的命令行，拿到它，你就可以认为约等于拿到了这台服务器的控制权了，所以这个名字的意思极其直接，从PHP，直通你的服务器。
它包含两个编号，CVE-2026-109618和CVE-2026-109619。
CVE你可以理解成漏洞的身份证号，全球统一。
严重程度用 CVSS 打分，满分10分，最开始泄露版本是满分，但是最后其实给的是9.2分。
要讲清楚这两个漏洞呢，还是得先说一个最近所有人都很肉疼的概念：
内存。
就是程序跑起来的时候，要不停地向系统“借”内存，用来存放临时数据，然后用完再“还”回去，PHP的解释器是用C语言写的，C语言跑得快，但借和还，依然全靠程序员自己记账，系统可不管你。
所以这个账一旦记错，就会出事了。
第一个漏洞，CVE-2026-109619，专业名词叫“释放后使用”（use-after-free）。
举个例子，你开了一家酒店，第一个客人来寄存行李，服务员把他的东西放进了18号柜子，并且在本子上记了下来。
后来客人走了，柜子清空，重新给第二个人用了。
结果问题来了，服务员忘记把本子上原来的记录删掉了。
第二个人刚把自己的东西放进去，服务员就拿着旧记录，跑去打开18号柜子，还以为里面是第一个人的行李。
这下就麻烦了，他可能看到了第二个人的东西，甚至还有可能把里面的东西给弄坏了。
PHP这次的问题，就出在类似的地方，原本已经归还的内存，又被拿去存放新的数据，但PHP还留着指向原来位置的旧记录。
于是，它以为自己在处理上一份数据，实际上碰到的早就成了另一份数据，所以，如果攻击者能精心操纵这个过程，就有机会读取、篡改原本不该碰的数据，甚至进一步控制服务器。
这就叫释放后使用，英文叫Use-After-Free。
轻一点，能读到服务器内存里别的用户的密码、令牌、API密钥，严重一点的话，精心布置内存以后，可以用你这台服务器，直接执行他自己的代码，那后果就不堪设想了。
第二个洞：内存不够时的紧急撤离，这是CVE-2026-109618。
这个漏洞更有意思，我们还是拿酒店举例。
假设酒店里有一个行李寄存处，每次客人过来寄存行李，服务员都要先在登记本上把数量加1，然后再把行李放到柜子里。
前面9件都很顺利，到了第10件，服务员刚刚把数量从9改成10，正准备放行李的时候。
突然一下，停电了，就导致行李还没放进去，整个系统就被迫中断了。
结果更离谱的来了，酒店启动紧急清理程序，清理人员拿着登记本一看：今天一共存了10件行李。
于是按照登记本上的数量，一个一个检查。
但问题是，第10件行李根本没放进去啊，那个位置里面可能还是一些乱七八糟的旧东西。

迈步“史上最大 IPO”，消息称 Anthropic 最快本周五公开提交上市申请
2026/10/22 10:17:14 来源： IT之家 作者： 清源 责编： 清源
评论：
感谢IT之家网友 华南吴彦祖 的线索投递！
IT之家 10 月 22 日消息，当地时间 21 日，据雅虎财经援引三名知情人士消息称，Anthropic 最早或于本周五公开提交 S-1 招股说明书，为有望创下史上最大规模的 IPO 迈出关键一步。
Anthropic 的上市计划备受关注，预计规模将超过 SpaceX 今年 6 月的 IPO 。随着投资者对 AI 行业巨额支出的担忧加剧，市场普遍认为，Anthropic 上市将成为检验投资者对 AI 热潮还有多大兴趣的一次重要考验。
今年 6 月，Anthropic 向美国证券交易委员会秘密提交了 IPO 申请草案。根据规定，采用保密申报程序的企业，须在正式投资者路演开始至少 15 个自然日前公开申请文件。
如果顺利公开招股书，Anthropic 距离 11 月上市 就将更近一步，但最终发行时间仍受市场环境等因素影响。届时，普通投资者也将首次得以了解其具体财务数据及潜在风险。
Anthropic 斥资数十亿美元建设 AI 基础设施，以支持 Claude 系列模型的训练和运行。除了与谷歌、亚马逊合作，公司还租用 SpaceX 旗下 Colossus 1 数据中心的 GPU 算力。
今年上半年，Anthropic 营收达到 163 亿美元 （IT之家注：现汇率约合 1,090.36 亿元人民币） ，净亏损超过 800 亿美元 （现汇率约合 5,351.46 亿元人民币） 。华尔街预计 Anthropic 可能通过 IPO 募资最多 1,000 亿美元 （现汇率约合 6,689.33 亿元人民币） ，对应估值高达 2 万亿美元 （现汇率约合 13.38 万亿元人民币） 。
另有消息称，Anthropic 上周在旧金山办公室向投资者透露，第三季度营收达到 168 亿美元 （现汇率约合 1,123.81 亿元人民币） ，高于第二季度的 115 亿美元 （现汇率约合 769.27 亿元人民币） 。按调整后口径计算，公司也实现了盈利。
一名知情人士称，Anthropic 的上市规模如此庞大，选择何时启动 IPO，也将对未来几周准备上市的其他企业产生重要影响。
竞争对手 OpenAI 原本预计今年启动 IPO，目前则预计于 2027 年初上市。

items.title: Anthropic 将 Agent Skills 开放标准捐赠给 Linux Foundation 旗下 Agentic AI Foundation
items.title_en: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.summary: Anthropic 宣布把 Agent Skills 开放标准捐赠给 Linux Foundation 旗下的 Agentic AI Foundation（AAIF），此前已向其捐赠 MCP。
items.fullContent:
Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Introducing Claude for Teachers
View more
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills , the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.
Agent interoperability through simplicity
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.
Donating Agent Skills to AAIF
We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.
We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.
Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.
What comes next
We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.
Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub .

A Mini App is a long-running application with a frontend and a backend. It installs as a plugin, calls and is called by the Agent, and keeps the Agent’s work on a page that stays live.
Today, we’re launching Mini App in the MiniMax Code desktop app. A Mini App is a long-running application with a frontend and a backend. It installs as a plugin, and it and the Agent can call each other. Our goal is to keep the Agent’s work on a page that stays live, instead of scattered across conversations.
A lot of work is already handed to Agents, from refactoring code to sorting through messages. But each task moves forward in its own conversation. Before picking one back up, you have to dig through a pile of conversations for the context and remember what that one was for. Asking the Agent for an HTML dashboard pulls the information into one place, but the page only shows the data from the moment it was generated. To keep it updated, push a task forward, or save results, you have to go back to the chat and explain everything again. Work between people and AI is never handed off just once: sometimes it needs a human’s revisions, and sometimes it needs the AI to pitch in.
Agent plugins let you change the Agent. Mini Apps let you build applications on top of it. System-level concerns like ports, the Agent, and the data directory belong to the host, MiniMax Code, which draws the boundaries between them. What the tool looks like is up to you: just tell the Agent.
Mini Apps
A Mini App is an extension compatible with the MiniMax Plugin protocol , with a miniapp.json manifest, a frontend, and a Node.js server added on top. The architecture is straightforward: the Node.js server fetches data, saves results, and exposes the app’s features to the Agent through hosted MCP. The page appears in the conversation sidebar and can pop out into its own window. Processes, ports, authentication, credentials, and rollback-capable publishing are all handled by the host.
Today’s release has three parts:
The Mini App runtime: a Node backend with a persistent data directory, hosted MCP, the Agent API, Host Connectors, and tool approvals handled right in the page
/miniapp-creator : go from a one-sentence request in chat to a working page
Official Mini Apps in the plugin marketplace, plus MiniMax-Code-MiniApps, the open-source community repository
With /miniapp-creator , the Agent first runs a read-only query against each data source to confirm it can get real data. Then it writes the page and the backend, publishes the app, opens it, and checks the result with screenshots in the built-in browser.
Several of the first official Mini Apps were built this way by colleagues outside our engineering team:
A stock dashboard Mini App brings stock information scattered across Knowledge Planet (Zsxq), Jinmen Finance, and Tencent Docs into a single dashboard.
CadQuery Viewer lets you mark positions on a 3D model and send them back to the conversation for the Agent to change.
Self-drive Route Planner combines map routing, place search, and image generation into one trip-planning workspace.
MiniMax Bot is itself a Mini App. The main bot assembles a team, hands long-running tasks to background Agent conversations, then reviews and reports on the results. Agents in those conversations can in turn call the Bot’s tools to send messages and to save and search memories. Most Bot updates only require a plugin change, with no need to wait for a MiniMax Code release. Its source code is now in the open-source community repository.
Developers in the open-source community have started building their own Mini Apps, too: a dashboard of token usage by date and model, Git Commit Tree for browsing Git history as a swimlane graph, and Session Trajectory for replaying a conversation’s model trajectory. Some lean toward everyday life and creative work, like Xinyu Island, for logging your mood and drawing a daily inspiration card, and Anatomy Gallery, where the Agent creates and edits interactive diagrams.
“From early workflows to RAG and Agentic Search, and inspired by our work at MiniMax, I’ve found that professional work needs something more than a flashy Agent: a native, tightly integrated environment where Agents and people work closely together. As a financial analyst, I used to spend most of my time pulling together scattered information. Now that Mini Apps bring it into my workspace, I can focus on thinking and judgment, and leave organizing, analyzing, and working through the information entirely to the Mini Apps.”
— Product Manager at MiniMax
On security: account credentials are held by the host, and neither plugins nor pages can access them. Connectors and Agent permissions must be declared in the manifest before they can be used. A Mini App’s server port is open only to its own pages and the Agent. When a page wants to pass something to the Agent, the content goes into your input box first, so you can review and edit it before sending. Mini App code runs on your machine as you, so only install packages from sources you trust.
Getting started
Mini Apps are available now in local sessions of the MiniMax Code desktop app (macOS / Windows).
You can install ready-made Mini Apps from the plugin marketplace, or describe what you need in chat and have the Agent build one on the spot. After using it for a while, ask the Agent to adjust it to the way you work.
To start building:
Download MiniMax Code: https://agent.minimax.io/download (mainland China: https://agent.minimax.cn/download )
Follow the quickstart to build your first Mini App with /miniapp-creator : https://agent.minimax.io/docs/miniapp/authors/quickstart
An open community
The source code for MiniMax Bot and the community’s Mini Apps all live in the open-source repository MiniMax-Code-MiniApps . If you’ve built a Mini App you find useful, we’d love for you to share it with a pull request.
If you need a runtime capability Mini Apps don’t have yet, leave a comment on the pinned capability wishlist in the community repository.

Oct 21, 2026, 1:57 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: The Verge
Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
OpenAI disclosed a pair of safety incidents that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks. In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled its safety monitor when copying reference code — and then lied about it.
“The reference didn’t configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user’s code,” Marcus Williams, an AI safety researcher at OpenAI, writes on X . “When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not.”
A separate incident occurred after a GPT-6.1 Sol agent suppressed automatic security alerts to OpenAI’s security team on Slack. In this case, the AI agent carried over an earlier instruction not to send any Slack messages to OpenAI’s team, using that to justify turning off the alerts.
Related
Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu
We’re running out of reasons to ignore AI safety
These incidents add to security concerns surrounding AI agents, some of which have circumvented their testing environment’s restrictions to hack outside companies. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI says. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.”

LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials | Wiz Blog
Wiz
Sign in
Under attack?
Get a demo
Benjamin Read , Rami McCarthy
October 21, 2026 |
LiteLLM Compromised
At 11:39 UTC on October 21, a malicious version (1.107.0) of the LiteLLM package was uploaded to PyPI. This version was quarantined on PyPI as of 13:20 UTC. According to ClickPy data , the malicious version received approximately 49,000 downloads.
LiteLLM Docker containers on GHCR and Docker hub also included the trojanized version of LiteLLM. These included the v1.107.0 , latest , main-latest and main-stable tags. These were removed ~13:53 UTC.
The most recent safe version is v1.106.2.
When the malicious package is installed, three files are extracted directly into the site-packages root: cook.pth , cook.py and sitecustomize.py . These packages are designed to be executed whenever a python interpreter is started.
Per LiteLLM developer BerriAI :
malicious actions were taken through three engineers' GitHub accounts, appearing to be by way of stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens. The threat actor used one user's account triggered the project-releaser run, and another user's account to approve it. All tokens which were involved in this attack have been revoked.
And in a followup :
GitHub CLI OAuth token exposure
After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs.
Access to our internal LiteLLM deployment
We identified an unexpected, innocuously named user account in our internal LiteLLM deployment, which was exposed to the public internet. We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow.
We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability.
UPDATES
14:05 UTC - added IOC table
14:15 UTC - added Attack Commits details
14:40 UTC - added Credential Stealer details, noted Docker takedown
15:20 UTC - clarified dual-technique approach novelty and LLM-aided development
16:40 UTC - added diagram of payload flow
16:55 UTC - added LiteLLM statement on root cause
18:35 UTC - LiteLLM has released a blog post
19:05 UTC - added observed post-exploitation activity
21:45 UTC - updated LiteLLM details on root cause
October 22 12:55 UTC - added PyPi download stats
Payload
Diagram of payload flow The payload has strong indications of LLM-aided development, including verbose variable names (encrypted_private_key_output ), overly defensive error handling with generic try/except blocks, platform-specific code paths that fail silently on untested platforms (Windows marker path /tmp/ doesn't exist, fcntl/fork calls crash the remote loader), and a dead code module ( exec_py ) that was defined but never called. The structure suggests iterative prompting: functional on the happy path but brittle at the edges and untested.
Upon startup, the interpreter processes cook.pth , which includes a command to import cook , which loads cook.py . cook.py deobfuscates itself, runs a stealer routine and writes a maker to /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb (note this fails on Windows, as the /tmp/ path often does not exist). The stealer routine gathers system, browser, developer, cloud and AI tool secrets, encrypts them and exfiltrates to www.litellm.dev/healthcheck via a post request. This domain is attacker controlled, impersonating LiteLLM infrastructure.
Python interpreters will also attempt to execute sitecustomize.py - however, it will only run on Linux & MacOS machines. This script attempts to fetch domain.txt from a GitHub dead drop ( letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt) . If it receives a response, it will attempt to download a second stage python script from http://<domain>/codepy and run it. As of the time of analysis, the domain.txt file was never populated beyond initial test values. The repo has been taken down by GitHub as of 1:30 PM UTC.
The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild.
Credential Stealer
The embedded credential stealer, internally named privcollect , harvests sensitive data across 16 modules targeting browsers, cloud providers, and AI services. It extracts:
browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari
AWS credentials from ~/.aws/ , environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS)
GCP service account keys and application default credentials
Azure tokens from the CLI cache
In terms of AI-specific theft, it targets API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers stored in environment variables or config files. It also collects SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files.
LiteLLM Proxy stores upstream API keys in a PostgreSQL database. The stealer queries this database directly ( SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable" LIMIT 500 ) to extract all configured provider credentials.
Harvested data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC (key wrapped with RSA-4096) and exfiltrated over HTTP to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck using the hardcoded X-Token header and an Internet Explorer 7 user-agent string.
Attacker Commits
The payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm . Note, this is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. This repository, not visible on GitHub, was used to inject the payload into the release pipeline.
Between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21, the attacker pushed 10 commits using the author email ckdi82fkoos@proton.me . The first nine commits were created on GitHub.com and therefore signed with GitHub's verified signature.
The first three (within 2 minutes) added the persistence files: cook.pth , cook.py , and sitecustomize.py . Four more commits bumped version numbers to 1.107.0 .
After a 39-minute gap, two commits refined the payload and added the critical data = "cook" directive to pyproject.toml , which instructed the build tool to bundle the malware into the wheel.
A final commit, made 58 minutes later with a different email ( Berri-AI@users.noreply.github.com ) and unsigned (suggesting a different environment), added COPY cook ./cook to the Dockerfiles.
Although the Berri-AI repository is unavailable, all commits remain accessible through the parent repository due to Git's fork object sharing. The full diff is available at: github.com/BerriAI/litellm/compare/a8113b0d...20535d8f
Post-Exploitation Activity
Wiz Research has observed abuse of stolen credentials , starting approximately 4.5 hours post-exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments, from the following IP addresses:
168.100.8[.]57
165.227.201[.]8
Each credential was checked with sts:GetCallerIdentity , followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels and a ListModels call, consistent with LLMjacking .
In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM ( ListRoles , ListUsers , ListAccessKeys ) and performed general discovery ( ListAccounts , DescribeTrails , etc.).
Recommendations
Wiz customers should review our Threat Intel Center advisory: Supply Chain Attack Targeting LiteLLM .
Indicators of Compromise
