items.fullContent:
MOFCOM's New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI
ChinaTalk
Subscribe Sign in
MOFCOM's New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI
a big deal
Quinn Ennis , Irene Zhang , Lily Ottinger , and Aqib Zakaria
Oct 21, 2026
57
4
12
Share
In the AI race thus far, openness has been China’s secret sauce. As fast followers to the frontier, Chinese AI companies have gained trust by publicizing their weights and architectures. And at the cost of revenue, they have achieved global adoption, brand recognition, and a truly competitive dynamic with American labs.
Last week, China’s Ministries of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Science and Technology (MOST) jointly proposed expanding China’s catalogue of export-controlled technologies, with most of the proposed regulations taking aim at subsets of China’s AI industry. Regulators will spend a month taking comments on the draft before anything becomes law, but we can already learn a ton from this announcement in its current form.
Does Beijing want to hold back the tides of open models? Why is MOFCOM writing these rules now, and what does this say about the Chinese government’s appetite for AI-enabled risks versus growth?
To find out, we spent three days poring over the draft regulations — so you don’t have to!
What’s ahead:
How these rules came to be — and how this draft is already affecting the Chinese AI industry;
What the proposed rules mean for frontier models, chip design, memory, cybersecurity, AI content detection, and even China’s minority languages;
Who actually decides which export licenses get approved, and the balance of power between provincial and central authorities;
What these rules tell us about Beijing’s expectations for AI development.
The 40 proposed additions in Announcement 48, split across AI, photovoltaics, and biomedicine.
Today, we’re just focusing on the AI-related regulations, but a future piece tackling everything else — from this announcement’s proposed restrictions on PV cells and gene therapies, to other recent announcements on port dredgers and tunnel borers — is in the works! Subscribe so you don’t miss it:
The Road to a Rule
Since 2001, MOFCOM has made regular additions to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export 中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录. In recent years, this catalogue has basically served to list the technologies for which China’s dominance in global production affords them leverage over the rest of the world — a toolbox of weaponizable dependencies, if you will. In the last several years, this has mostly meant processing and manufacturing technologies for rare earths, magnets, and battery materials.
Now China has decided AI models belong on that list as well. On October 16, MOFCOM released Announcement 48 of 2026, detailing 40 new additions to the Catalogue and, effective immediately, requiring pre-export registration of all 40 additions in the interim. Of these 40 additions, 14 are outright export prohibitions (J codes), while 26 are export restrictions requiring licenses (X codes). 1
It’s a bad day to be working at MOFCOM. Meme template from Chicken Chop Bro .
While these 40 additions have garnered the majority of public attention, equally important is the section of the announcement creating an interim pre-export registration system. From last Friday to the date that the revised Catalogue takes effect, any technology exporter must register any exports of technologies among the above additions prior to export, including exports that have already begun but not yet completed (已经开始但尚未完成). There is no precedent in any earlier catalogue revision for the creation of an interim registration regime announced with draft additions. Beijing is creating a better dataset so that it can make an informed final decision on what to license.
Under Announcement 48, registration is required for a Chinese company hoping to: 1) assign ownership of the technology abroad, like in the case of an IP sale, 2) license domestic technology abroad, 3) change the owner or actual controller of domestic technology to a foreign entity, or 4) do anything else that MOFCOM later decides to specify. The triggers for registration also suggest that MOFCOM is testing what mechanisms will ultimately be used for classification of an AI export. An AI model is not a physical item like a gallium ingot, so the question of what constitutes export is less clear.
This third trigger effectively codifies the Manus case . In December 2025, Meta signed a deal to purchase Manus, a Chinese agent startup that had moved to Singapore, but following MOFCOM review, a security review led by the NDRC led to the deal being reversed. Now, rather than relying on investment review authority, similar deals would require a license on export control grounds, and redomiciliation would not let a company escape Chinese jurisdiction.
In the registration form provided with the announcement, MOFCOM asks for standard information like the recipient, technology code, user and end use, and secrecy grade. It also asks for specific circumstances of exports not made under contract (不依据合同出口的具体情形). This forces exporters to judge for themselves whether they should report a potential action, and may point to open-sourcing and sharing code within a group.
IP and National Security
These rules fall into two categories: controls that protect intellectual property (IP), and controls that protect state security.
To Xi Jinping, these are not separate justifications. As he explained during a 2020 study session speech , “Intellectual property protection weighs on national security; only by strictly protecting intellectual property can we effectively safeguard our country’s independently developed key core technologies and prevent and resolve major risks.” (“知识产权保护工作关系国家安全，只有严格保护知识产权，才能有效保护我国自主研发的关键核心技术、防范化解重大风险。”)
We’ll start with the controls that seem primarily IP-focused (frontier models, AI chip design, memory chips, and clusters), then move on to controls in the middle (AI-generated content detectors and agents), and finish on the primarily state security-focused controls (training data, cyber capabilities, and in a suprise addition minority languages!).
Controls by Type
Frontier models
When you use a frontier U.S. model, you are accessing the software without getting a peek at the fundamental structure behind the curtain, and thus closed models can be used without directly leaking IP. Most of China’s domestic AI champions, however, publish open weight models, meaning that the user can see the structure of the model, and much of the IP is fundamentally public. Open weight, though, does not mean open source, and the training data, preprocessing pipelines, and training code remain behind the curtain.
MOFCOM proposes to require licenses for the export of both weights and core private IP, including key checkpoints, underlying source code, architecture design, and technology for training optimization and inference acceleration. The regulation controls the core technology of a large model that exceeds any of the following three thresholds: ≥10 26 floating point operations, ≥2T parameters, or “global leading capability” 能力达到全球领先水平. We discuss each threshold here:
≥10 26 floating point operations (FLOPs)
The number of floating point operations (FLOP) is a common measure of the raw compute used to train an AI model, and is thus often a good proxy for model performance. The minimum cutoff listed in this MOFCOM announcement is identical to the figure originally mentioned in a 2023 Biden executive order , which was later used in the January 2025 AI Diffusion rule ( US ECCN 4E091 ) that was rescinded in May 2025. This is also the same threshold as California SB 53 . In its follow-up Q&A, MOFCOM mentioned “referencing internationally accepted standards” 参考国际通行做法 while drafting these proposed catalogue additions. As of October 20, 2026, no released Chinese model is estimated to have crossed this bar. The Chinese models with the largest training compute sit at roughly 2x10 25 FLOP, according to Epoch AI . China remains compute-constrained compared to the United States.
≥2T parameters
The number of parameters in a model is the overall size of the model, which is a rough proxy for its capability. As of now, per Epoch AI, only four Chinese models since mid-2024 (Kimi K3, ERNIE 5.0, Qwen 3.8 Max, and Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B) cross this threshold. No models from DeepSeek, Meituan, Xiaomi, or Z.ai exceed two trillion parameters, but all have models above or near one trillion parameters, and it is reasonable to expect their next releases to cross that threshold. As the Q&A clarified, the restriction does not cover tech that is already public via open weights or literature, so there is an incentive for companies to rush new releases that would exceed the thresholds before the rule is final (I do wonder how MOFCOM feels about DeepInfer, probably positively but did they get the nod beforehand?). This test is especially important for Chinese labs as China is compute constrained, and compute-scarce labs often use a design called Mixture of Experts (MoE), creating large models that only activate a small fraction of their network for any given task. If you measure these models by FLOPs used in training, it undercounts their power and makes them look weaker than they are. Total parameters, while a much better proxy for the Chinese frontier, has a potential weakness: the number of parameters is a design choice, so labs could try to game it by releasing models that slide under the 2T threshold.
Global leading level
This category is by far the most up-for-interpretation. The note states that the bar is the global top 10 through public evaluations from “mainstream domestic and foreign testing organizations and large-scale industrial platforms” 国内外主流测评机构，大规模产业平台 across “overall performance, specialized operational capabilities, global call volume, safety performance, training efficiency or others” 综合性能，专项业务能力，全球调用量，安全性能，训练效率， 等. This definition allows the rule to cover a wide range of models. The rule does not name a ranking body, and, in practice, different AI ranking bodies frequently disagree on their ordering as they use different tests and rating algorithms. Likewise, the rule would potentially affect any model that was in a top-10 list on any one dimension, even if the criteria were narrow. The mention of call volume also has the potential to pull in weaker models that are used in high volume for easier tasks. Given that the status is judged at time of export, it is likely that the same model could jump off or on a leaderboard between subsequent exports without the model itself changing.
Left: How current Chinese models measure up to Announcement 48’s size and compute tests. Some models lack public compute estimates. Right: How top Chinese and U.S. models compare on one public benchmark naming — the draft rule names no specific ranking.
The carve-out for already-released open source models means that published weights are out of the scope of this control, but closed-weight model companies hoping to license existing models to foreign firms and future releases by open-weight companies would still be restricted under the proposed rule. Just because a model is open weight, it does not mean it is open source. Open weight companies still hold private know-how, and this IP related to training is directly controlled by a clause mentioning training optimization and inference acceleration 训练优化、推理加速. Open sourcing a restricted model is a controlled export and would get an automatic license.
AI chip design
The announcement proposes restricting the export of AI chip design that checks off at least one of the following boxes:
requires a manufacturing process of 14 nm or below;
is able to do floating-point or integer arithmetic;
uses advanced 2.5D or 3D packaging to integrate multiple dies;
has high-speed interconnect capacity;
has an architecture integrating memory and compute;
or is used in autonomous driving, computer vision, or speech.
The inclusion of any chips with floating-point or integer arithmetic capabilities 具备浮点或整型运算能力 means that this covers almost all digital chips, including all AI chips, which suggests either a drafting error or an extremely wide breadth (MOFCOM will probably be getting some polite letters around this clause…). Likewise, all AI chips used in datacenters require high-speed interconnect capability to interface with other chips and memory.
The inclusion of architectures that integrate memory and compute is also noteworthy. Traditionally, AI chips use von-Neumann architecture, where memory and compute are housed separately and data moves back and forth between the processor and the memory. This shuttling of the data wastes energy, however, and technologies like in-memory and neuromorphic computing, explicitly mentioned in the announcement, eliminate this energy loss and allow for greater parallelism. Non-von-Neumann architectures would also potentially allow China to circumvent its shortage of traditional high-bandwidth memory (HBM). While these technologies have seen limited deployment in datacenters because the technology is immature and lacks a mature software ecosystem, they have been used in smaller research data centers and are used in robotics, drones, and autonomous vehicles. China is highly competitive across these three sectors. Indeed, when paired with the direct inclusion of chips used in autonomous driving and computer vision, this gestures to a strategic vision. For Beijing, protecting its advantage in memory-integrated chips could help it plan a future data center build-out that is not dependent on Western memory supply chains.
This forward-looking export control on a technology that has not yet picked up real adoption is also reminiscent of the FCC’s own Robot Ban . No one is really sure whether these technologies will take off, but given they are not yet widespread, the easiest time to restrict them is now. The market being hit is minimal, and companies that design such chips don’t have large vested interests to protest against the rule. In the case that non-von-Neumann architectures find commercial viability in the future, China will not have to worry about the US profiting off designs and IP; that door would have already been shut.
This restriction, and the following restriction on memory chip technology, does not restrict the chips themselves. Chinese companies remain free to sell AI chips and the memory used in data centers to U.S. companies. The restriction instead applies to the intellectual property associated with these chips, allowing Beijing to have a say in patent deals with foreign companies.
This design control can also be construed as MOFCOM disallowing Chinese companies from fabbing their designs at TSMC or other companies. While BIS has attempted to play the cat-and-mouse game to prevent Chinese AI chip designers from covertly sending their designs to TSMC, MOFCOM may be cracking down on Chinese companies itself. Time will tell how the rule ultimately gets enforced: is it more about protecting Chinese designs, or forcing Chinese designers to work with Chinese, not Taiwan or American, fabs?
Memory chips
This MOFCOM announcement further focuses on memory with its proposed restriction of memory chip design technology export. This restriction’s use of an “any of the following” structure creates a broad category under the guise of narrow delineations. The restrictions on 3D flash (long-term memory) and DRAM (short-term, working memory) design are not AI-specific, capturing much of the memory work at YMTC and CXMT. For a brief refresher on memory, see Aqib’s excellent primer on Chinese HBM.
Many of the limbs of the restriction allow broad interpretation. For both types of memory, the proposed addition would require export licenses for all memory that uses bonding technology to join separately made chip layers. This would cover every flash chip made by YMTC as well as almost all HBM chips, which are further covered by the mention of any chips using multi-layer stacking. For flash, the announcement includes density (8 Gb/mm 2 ) and speed (1.5 Gbps I/O) minima that both fall well below current mainstream chips. Likewise, for DRAM, the restriction would apply to any designs requiring a manufacturing process below 18 nm, which would include almost all CXMT DRAM.
These numbers are copied over directly from Biden-era regs. The 18 nm DRAM cutoff is the exact threshold used by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) October 2022 export controls on memory! This BIS control also included a line on flash, restricting chips with 128 layers or more. When converted from layers to density, 2 this is almost exactly the limit proposed in this MOFCOM announcement. On the surface, this symmetry with Washington can be seen as preparing a ready-made defense for these restrictions as “standard international practice.” This can also be viewed, however, as fencing off the IP that China has built in the last four years because of those BIS controls — a protection of the dividend from its forced indigenization of these technologies.
Another inclusion worth noting is DRAM technology that uses vertical channel transistors (VCT). Where traditional memory cells are laid flat, in VCT the cells are stood upright, allowing for more memory in the same space without requiring higher precision lithography. China has invested heavily in this technology, as it presents a potential to circumvent Western denial of access to fabrication technologies like EUV. Indeed, in the week before the draft, CXMT announced that it would release a VCT design that shrinks the footprint of each memory cell from the mainstream level by a third by the end of 2026. This prompted a drop in the stock prices of both Samsung and SK hynix, both of which have targeted 2028 for their release of VCT memory. Both Samsung and SK hynix could have pursued VCT earlier but ultimately decided to squeeze more juice out of EUV before turning to VCT. When they do transition, however, the process will inevitably take time as the companies struggle to reach appropriate yield with a new design. China does not want to give the big memory makers any shortcut with that trial and error, as China has learned from the footsteps of other companies. By controlling VCT, China is hoping that the Korean companies will face the same yield struggles as CXMT.
Clusters
US chip controls have forced China to compete through workarounds, and now, Chinese firms have gotten good enough at engineering whole alternative systems for compute that the government believes they have domestic IP worth protecting. Areas where China could have a comparative advantage include wiring many weaker chips into superPoDs like Huawei’s CloudMatrix 384 , engineering systems to keep running through failures, and mixing Nvidia and domestic fleets as one. This corresponds directly to this announcement’s proposed restriction on the export of technology relating to large clusters (≥10,000 AI accelerators) with either fast interconnect (≥800 GB/s), fast recovery from failures (≤120 s), high scaling efficiency (≥98%), or unified scheduling across chips from at least two vendors.
This rule would protect such comparative advantages by giving automatic licenses to self-built, self-operated overseas data centers of Chinese firms, while exercising real bureaucratic scrutiny over prospective sales of the tech and IP licensing agreements. That could be used to push companies in the Gulf and Southeast Asia to rent Chinese compute rather than buy it, as the hardware could be freely sold but the know-how to build or run them without Chinese engineers is gated by the licensing desk. Even though China doesn’t have enough chips today to export, this would seem to make the ‘Chinese stack’ less attractive going forward.
Agents
The proposed agent restrictions were inspired by the debacle with Meta’s attempted acquisition of Manus, aiming to formalize the authority to block future transactions.
Chinese firms already sell agent products abroad (from well-known tools like Manus and Kimi , to specialized platforms like Alibaba’s Accio Work ), and they could continue to do so under the proposed changes — but they will now need a license to allow the client to host and manage the agent reasoning loop in their own environment.
The agent capabilities that trigger the restrictions (autonomous planning/task decomposition, multi-agent collaboration, and tool use) are not necessarily unique to Chinese firms , and the thresholds in each of these qualifying capabilities seem somewhat arbitrary (e.g., integration of 200 third-party tools). But the Manus sale indicates that Chinese firms do have valuable IP when it comes to agents, so we can think of these controls as applying to the specific architectures that enable Chinese agent products to hit these thresholds while keeping costs comparatively low.
The fourth capability proposed for export restriction is “AI decision-making technology for strategic interactions” (人工智能博弈决策技术), e.g., wargaming and game-theoretic AI. 3 Controlling those capabilities is, of course, more in line with the state security justification than with IP protection.
Spoiler? Show less Multiagent collaboration tech would be restricted if the overall task completion time is at most “two times the minimum completion time of a single agent” (“整体任务完成时间≤单智能体最低完成时间2倍”). We’re wondering if that wording is intentional, as it allows the multi-agent system to be twice as slow as a single agent. Technical folks, are we missing something here? We’ll be watching to see if this wording makes it into the final draft.
AI-generated content detection tools
The proposed controls also cover exports of advanced AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors. Detection tools with accuracy above 98% are in the restricted category and will be exportable with a license. But detection tools used by Chinese authorities, in relation to national security threats and content entering China from abroad, are outright prohibited from being exported if their accuracy rate exceeds just 95%. The exact wording covers tools that are “specifically or primarily used to prevent and address security risks in China’s cross-border network-data transmission ” “专门或者主要用于 我国网络数据跨境传输安全风险 防范和处置” — data security seems to be the most important threat. This makes intuitive sense: proprietary censorship tools used by state authorities are presumably trained on sensitive data, so as to be able to detect content that Beijing deems noteworthy. Therefore, exports of these tools run the risk of leaking political secrets or enabling an adversary to reverse-engineer AI-generated political content that these tools are less likely to detect.
But why require export licenses for AIGC detectors not used by the government? To Lily, it seems MOFCOM believes that China could have valuable IP here. Chinese social media platforms are, in theory, required by law to detect and label AIGC, so perhaps this is an area where Chinese companies are doing hardcore innovation and will eventually develop commercially competitive products. RedNote has published research on AI image detection, although it’s not clear how much of their AIGC detection algorithms for audio, video, and images are developed in-house vs. by an external model maker. Other platforms are similarly tight-lipped about their AIGC labeling systems. Curiously, few competitive AI-generated text detectors have come out of China: even a recent state media editorial on AIGC, reprinted by Xinhua, mentioned Pangram and GPTZero as example detectors, seemingly unable to name local equivalents. So congratulations to Pangram on ascending to national security crown jewel status.
Ceding the international market would be bad news for profitability and product quality. If authorities are restrictive in licensing detection products — or if there is a risk your license won’t be renewed because your detection algorithm became so good that the government decided to start using it — that could make tech companies hesitant to spend resources improving these tools.
Training data
In addition to restricting the export of large models, the proposed revisions to the Catalogue cover all AI models trained on sensitive data, regardless of size or performance. The inclusion logic here rests on security rather than IP. Model weights hold the potential to act as a channel to move data outside of China, so Beijing plans to regulate them as an extension of China’s existing rules on data leaving the country.
The rule completely bans the export of models trained on “core data” 核心数据, and restricts the export of those trained on “important data” 重要数据. These categories come from China’s Data Security Law . “Core data” includes any data on national security, economic lifelines, important livelihoods, or major public interests 关系国家安全、国民经济命脉、重要民生、重大公共利益. “Important data,” on the other hand, is left for “relevant regions and departments” to define and catalogue.

items.title: Wiz Research 披露 PHP2Shell：AI 助攻 PHP 核心 RCE 漏洞，影响全球 70% 网站
items.title_en: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
items.summary: Wiz Research 披露 PHP 核心中的多个内存安全漏洞（CVE-2026-109618/109619，CVSS 最高 9.2），实现无需认证的远程代码执行与内存泄露，影响至少追溯到 PHP 5.4 的近十年版本。
items.fullContent:
PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet | Wiz Blog
Wiz
Sign in
Under attack?
Get a demo
Sagi Tzadik , Shir Tamari , Nir Ohfeld , Tomer Schwartz
October 21, 2026 |
Executive Summary
Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.
PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.
These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it , putting every affected website in immediate risk.
Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.
On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine.
These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability  required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.
Overview
In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.
Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.
PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.
Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.
Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.
We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare , Fastly , Google , Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel , and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.
The Vulnerabilities
All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.
Below you can find a table that demonstrates what type of impact was demonstrated by each of the bugs we reported to PHP. The applications listed below are targets we chose for the RCE demonstrations. They are representative targets - exploitation does not require one of these CMSs, as the vulnerable code is in PHP itself.
Tracking ID Bug What an attacker can achieve What we demonstrated CVE-2026-109618 Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free
Remote process-memory disclosure
Corrupt process memory and execute code
Unauthenticated disclosure of PHP worker memory
Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla
Application-agnostic remote memory disclosure
CVE-2026-109619 Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free
OPcache type confusion
Corrupt process memory and execute code
Corrupt shared PHP state and execute code
Pre-authentication RCE on Drupal
Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress
While this blog covers only four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs) that follow this problematic pattern, there are other tracked, and likely untracked, variants of this issue in the PHP codebase. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release.
Impact
We combined these vulnerabilities into a single exploit script, php2shell, and demonstrated that it could execute code remotely without authentication on deployments of WordPress ( wordpress:latest ), Drupal ( drupal:latest ), and Joomla ( joomla:latest ), using their latest container images at the time of testing.
These platforms illustrate the impact, but the vulnerabilities are in PHP itself. Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.
Separately, we demonstrated that attackers could read sensitive data from the PHP process’s memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys, without needing to achieve remote code execution.
Demonstrations of PHP2Shell with Wordpress, Joomla, and Drupal:
The AI inflection point
The vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Turning these flaws into working exploits required chaining multiple bugs and accounting for how PHP allocates and reuses memory across requests. Memory bugs are notoriously complex; differences in PHP versions, configurations and application behavior can break assumptions the exploit depends on. An attack that works against one deployment may need substantial adjustments to work against another, each requiring further analysis, testing and debugging. Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale.
With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts. With testing and debugging tools, models can analyze failures and iterate on adjustments, reducing the specialist effort required for each target. This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments.
This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets.
We used Wiz Atlas , Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research. Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.
Using Gemini 4 Argon, the team at Wiz has shown why frontier AI is a game-changer for cyber defense. For over a decade, these critical vulnerabilities remained unaddressed because vulnerability discovery and exploitation were incredibly complex. We're pleased to see Gemini 4 Argon help defenders bridge that gap, finding vulnerabilities and helping patch them.
Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind
Industry-level collaborations
Prior to public disclosure, Wiz Research worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI on discovery, coordination and patch verification. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately.
A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application. PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.
Technical deep dive
Bug: Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free
PHP's Session module can decode session data during upload-progress handling in the same pre-initialization window. The decoder stores request-owned bookkeeping in BG(unserialize) . A fatal allocation failure can interrupt this path, destroy the request heap and leave the unserializer's global state published.
On a later request handled by the same worker, PHP can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live unserializer bookkeeping. The stale state becomes a powerful memory-corruption primitive. We combined it with the memory disclosure to remove address uncertainty and achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.
The WordPress, Drupal and Joomla chains are representative demonstrations. The underlying primitives exist at the PHP engine level and can affect any PHP application running on a vulnerable version.
These issues execute below the application layer, so application logs may contain little context. Until systems are patched, defenders should pay particular attention to unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These signals can guide an investigation. Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation.
Bug: Remote process-memory disclosure
PHP parses RFC1867 multipart requests during request startup, before normal module initialization has completed. Session upload-progress handling can initialize Session state at this early stage and publish a session ID in PS(id) . An out-of-memory error can abort the request before cleanup completes. PHP then destroys the request heap and may leave PS(id) pointing to the freed allocation.
A later multipart request handled by the same worker can reach the upload-progress cleanup path before normal Session initialization resets that pointer. PHP trusts the stale pointer and length as a live zend_string and URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The attack works even when the application never calls session_start() , making the issue application-agnostic. We demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of an attacker-sized region of live worker memory containing data from outside the attacker's request.
Bug: Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free
In affected versions, PHP retains the backtrace of the most recent fatal error in EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace) . A fatal out-of-memory error can destroy the request heap without undefining that executor-global value. The worker survives with a global that still points to memory from the previous request.
If the same worker emits a diagnostic early in the next request, it can access the pointer before the executor reinitializes that state. PHP then destroys or updates the dangling backtrace and follows attacker-reclaimed memory. The resulting cross-request use-after-free can be developed into controlled memory corruption. We demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against Drupal using this primitive.
Bug: OPcache type confusion
OPcache persists compiled PHP structures in shared memory and assigns indices into per-worker runtime-pointer maps. Workers coordinate those indices through a shared frontier. During zend_accel_script_persist() , PHP advances the process-local CG(map_ptr_last) frontier. It publishes the corresponding shared frontier only after persistence completes. An allocation failure between those two events leaves the process-local advance in place and partially persisted objects referring to slots that the shared state still considers available.
When another worker later reuses one of those slots for a different runtime object, stale shared metadata resolves to a pointer of the wrong type. The mismatch creates a cross-worker type confusion and corrupts shared OPcache state. We used this primitive to build an unauthenticated RCE chain against WordPress.
There are other variants outside of these four bugs. While we initially reported these four to PHP, through this research we realized the vulnerability is deeply rooted in the PHP codebase and will require a comprehensive fix. Other variants should also fold under the same two CVEs.
How Can Wiz Help?
Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intel Center advisory for PHP2Shell , which includes built-in coverage for agentless and runtime vulnerability detection, exploitation detection via Wiz Defend and Sensor, and automatic response policies, alongside remediation and threat hunting guidance.
Sensor customers using the newest version (1.0.12768) can also enable a built-in response policy to automatically terminate processes exhibiting behaviors typical of PHP2Shell exploitation:
Conclusion
With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated. It marks an AI inflection point. The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit. With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work.
This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. Vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. These same capabilities also give defenders a chance to uncover and fix flaws that have survived years of scrutiny.
Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research, with Argon making a particularly significant contribution to finding and helping to remediate the vulnerability.
The opportunity is to make this work routine: systematically finding flaws in existing software and catching new ones before they reach production. Our coordinated efforts with PHP, OpenAI and Calif advance that goal, applying AI to strengthen the software foundations we all share.
Responsible disclosure timeline
August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.
August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.

X 上的 Rohan Paul：“Main takeaways from SpaceX’s earnings call today
> AI is now SpaceX’s biggest business: The Super Intelligence segment, which rents computing capacity to customers including Anthropic and Google, brought in $7.6B, nearly triple its $2.56B in the second quarter.
That made it SpaceX’s largest revenue source, ahead of the $5.2B Starlink connectivity business, with $608M coming from the newly acquired Cursor.
> SpaceX swung to a profit: Net income reached $4.4B on $14.6B of revenue, up 161%, against a $1.1B loss a year earlier and a $541M loss in the second quarter. Even so, SpaceX still showed a $413M net loss for the first 9 months of 2026.
> A SpaceX-Tesla merger is under study: Committees of independent directors at both companies are discussing a combination at shareholders’ request, and Musk said he is excluded from those talks as a conflicted party. He called a merger a good idea but said it isn’t certain, and any deal would need support from a majority of all outstanding Tesla shares.
> Musk sees revenue multiplying: Musk projected annual recurring revenue of $500B to $1T by the end of 2027. SpaceX’s own guidance is far lower in the near term, with $100B in annualized revenue by the end of 2026, based on December sales, and $33B to $37B of revenue in the first quarter of 2027.
> Spending is outrunning revenue: Capital spending hit $19.6B in the third quarter, $16.4B of it in the AI segment, and SpaceX expects $35B to $40B in the fourth quarter. Musk said SpaceX prefers short-term compute contracts because he expects each watt of computing to earn more as AI models improve.
> Musk is working from Memphis: Musk said he often spends 4 days a week in Memphis bringing the Colossus II supercomputer online, as SpaceX adds roughly 200K Nvidia GB300 chips a month. Compute capacity stood at 1.7GW at the end of September, SpaceX expects 2.5GW to 3GW by year-end, and Musk said he is confident of adding 10GW during 2027.
> Louisiana launches are expected by 2029: SpaceX recently announced plans for a $100B spaceport in Louisiana, and Musk said the internal goal is a first launch there within 2 years, while 2029 is highly likely, with launches at scale that year.”

> SpaceX swung to a profit: Net income reached $4.4B on $14.6B of revenue, up 161%, against a $1.1B loss a year earlier and a $541M loss in the second quarter. Even so, SpaceX still showed a $413M net loss for the first 9 months of 2026.
> A SpaceX-Tesla merger is under study: Committees of independent directors at both companies are discussing a combination at shareholders’ request, and Musk said he is excluded from those talks as a conflicted party. He called a merger a good idea but said it isn’t certain, and any deal would need support from a majority of all outstanding Tesla shares.
> Musk sees revenue multiplying: Musk projected annual recurring revenue of $500B to $1T by the end of 2027. SpaceX’s own guidance is far lower in the near term, with $100B in annualized revenue by the end of 2026, based on December sales, and $33B to $37B of revenue in the first quarter of 2027.
> Spending is outrunning revenue: Capital spending hit $19.6B in the third quarter, $16.4B of it in the AI segment, and SpaceX expects $35B to $40B in the fourth quarter. Musk said SpaceX prefers short-term compute contracts because he expects each watt of computing to earn more as AI models improve.
> Musk is working from Memphis: Musk said he often spends 4 days a week in Memphis bringing the Colossus II supercomputer online, as SpaceX adds roughly 200K Nvidia GB300 chips a month. Compute capacity stood at 1.7GW at the end of September, SpaceX expects 2.5GW to 3GW by year-end, and Musk said he is confident of adding 10GW during 2027.
> Louisiana launches are expected by 2029: SpaceX recently announced plans for a $100B spaceport in Louisiana, and Musk said the internal goal is a first launch there within 2 years, while 2029 is highly likely, with launches at scale that year.

items.title: Anthropic 开启 Claude Duet 研究预览，Claude 以主动式智能体接管日常工作
items.title_en: Introducing Claude Duet
items.summary: Anthropic 开启 Claude Duet 研究预览，一款让 Claude 作为主动式智能体工作的独立应用，已登陆 iOS、Android 和 claude.ai，面向美国 Pro 和 Max 用户开放候补名单。
items.fullContent:
Introducing Claude Duet | Claude by Anthropic
Skip to main content
Contact sales Try Claude
Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track.
It’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. For this research preview, Claude Duet is included in Pro and Max plans and uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. To get access, join the waitlist (opens in new tab) .
Put your attention where it matters most
We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before.
What makes Claude Duet so helpful is its judgment. We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5 (opens in new tab) and built it to be resourceful and to decide what needs you, what can wait, and when to check with you first.
Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.
Safety and discretion are built in
Claude Duet draws on years of security, safety, and privacy work on agents, both our own and the infrastructure businesses use to run theirs:
Claude Duet draws on our framework for trustworthy agents (opens in new tab) , which also guides agents like Claude Code and Claude in Chrome.
Claude Duet’s handling of credentials follows the design we use for Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) , so it never directly sees your passwords or sign-in tokens.
Actions are approved by our auto mode classifier (opens in new tab) , the same safeguard that protects Claude and Claude Code from taking steps you didn’t ask for.
Claude Duet’s defenses against hidden instructions and prompt injection come from our browser-use research (opens in new tab) , and our models and safeguards also cover this more broadly.
We run adversarial tests for Claude Duet’s security infrastructure. Red teams and an external firm penetration tested Claude Duet, and it’s covered by our public bug bounty program (opens in new tab) .
How Claude Duet handles sensitive information. We’re also releasing Claude Duet with a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt that checks each message and guards against leaks of sensitive information. An agent that reads email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where information should go. This new classifier and prompt are designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health or personal finances, are let through only when you’ve explicitly instructed Claude Duet to send it.
We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections, and will share more details about how Claude Duet is designed for safety in the coming days.
How testers are using Claude Duet
People at Anthropic have been using Claude Duet to accomplish more, but also to leave more room for thinking and being present. Boris Cherny, who leads our Claude Code team, talks through his mental to-do list with Claude Duet on walks, instead of saving the work for his desk. Chelsea Larsson, who leads our model and product behavior design team, hands Claude Duet her to-do list before leaving to be with her kids and it saves the results for an evening report. And the team behind Claude Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews, partner with him on prototypes, and even ship code.
We gave small business owners and entrepreneurs early access to Claude Duet, and some have been using it to help run their businesses. Here’s what some of them said:
Jess gets a rundown from Claude Duet each morning. One day, without being asked, it flagged a property showing that was on her calendar for the wrong day. “[This is] exactly the kind of thing I want caught without having to ask,” she said.
Jess Provencher, broker and owner, Pro Homes
Amin owns Shahs of Kabob in South Florida with about 110 employees. He’s used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support, and marketing, and has worked through his invoices store by store. “It brings it all together,” he said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.”
Amin Ebrahimi, owner, Shahs of Kabob
Mya had a call coming up with a potential client. Claude Duet saw it on her calendar and prepared a brief. It also noticed the call fell right before her flight and offered to move it. “I didn’t realize that it was right before my flight,” she said. “I love that proactivity.”
Mya Dalton, a brand strategist
How Claude Duet works
Your context from Claude is the foundation. Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work. What changes is how you work together: Claude Duet comes to you first, and you can message it through typing or voice in one ongoing thread, so a quick reply and a weeklong project both start in the same place.
Work continues when you step away. Claude Duet has a virtual machine with its own browser, so it doesn’t require your laptop or phone to be on. Describe a task in a short message, and it works out which apps to use and what steps to take in the background. You’ll receive a notification when the task is complete or needs your review.
Receive a message when something needs you. Claude Duet checks your connected accounts every few hours, because checking nonstop would use up your plan’s limits much faster. We’re continuing to test its judgment about when to message you, and we’ll keep tuning it based on what testers tell us. You can also tell it what you want to hear about and how often.
Important decisions stay with you. Claude Duet reads, drafts, and prepares work on its own. But before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your approval. A few things are off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities or moving money between accounts. You’re also able to disconnect any app Claude Duet has access to.
Connect with the tools your business runs on. Claude Duet can use the over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace (opens in new tab) to:
Find the Gmail and Slack messages you’ve missed and help you reply.
Check Intuit QuickBooks or Stripe for unpaid invoices and draft reminders.
Prepare and run payroll in Gusto, with hours, bonuses, and reimbursements filled in.
Draft a job posting and, once you edit and approve, post it to LinkedIn.
Help prepare agreements and send them for review and signature through Docusign.
Draft follow-up emails using the contact and deal history in HubSpot.
Turn your product launch into a social campaign in Canva.
Set up, design, and manage your Shopify store. Coming soon, a richer visual editor will let you design your storefront and preview it before anything goes live.
You can also use Claude Duet to purchase things for your business using Link, Stripe’s digital wallet. Claude Duet confirms the item with you, and Link asks you to approve the spend. It then pays with a virtual card, so your real card number isn’t shared. It can also use Shop Pay from Shopify to check out at online stores. Coming soon, with your permission, it will be able to sign in to sites with logins you’ve saved in 1Password.
Join the research preview
This is an early version of Claude Duet, and it still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent. We built its core functionality around work, so personal errands, such as booking tickets, aren’t quite as strong, and it can’t yet show you its browser. For now, Claude Duet lives in its own app, separate from the main Claude app. What we learn from early users will shape how the two work together.
During the research preview, Claude Duet shares your plan’s usage limits with the rest of Claude, and it uses them differently than a typical conversation does. Its background checks count toward those limits, and larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, require more model turns and background work.
We’re starting today with Pro and Max users in the US. Join the waitlist (opens in new tab) and we’ll email as soon as Claude Duet’s ready for you.

items.title: 蚂蚁集团与 vLLM 社区开源量化推理内核库 Humming
items.title_en: Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference
items.summary: 蚂蚁集团与 vLLM 社区开源通用高性能量化推理内核库 Humming，仓库为 github.com/vllm-project/humming。
items.fullContent:
Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog
Menu
Theme
Table of Contents
Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features:
Broad device support : Supports NVIDIA GPU architectures from Turing onward, along with CUDA-compatible devices such as T-Head's Zhenwu 810E.
Extensive quantization support : A unified architecture supports diverse combinations of weight and activation formats for dense and MoE workloads, covering a wide range of integer and floating-point types, bit widths, and scaling schemes.
Strong execution performance : Significantly outperforms existing implementations from vLLM Marlin, FlashInfer, and DeepGEMM across many representative workloads.
Repository: github.com/vllm-project/humming
Background
As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency.
Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space.
These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low.
Developing and integrating a dedicated kernel for every combination creates a growing maintenance burden. Each addition can require its own weight preprocessing, kernel selection, framework adapters, and tests. Optimizations must then be carried across multiple implementations.
Humming addresses this problem by separating quantization descriptions from execution choices and composing kernels from shared components.
General-Purpose Architecture
Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components.
A Unified Quantization Representation
Models exported by different quantization tools vary in numeric format, parameter organization, and weight layout. Humming converts supported export formats into the Humming standard format: a common quantization description with consistently organized weights, scales, zero points, and other tensors.
This representation preserves each scheme's quantization semantics while describing weight format, scaling granularity, scale data type, zero points, and secondary scales as separate parameters. Activations have their own numeric format and quantization settings. These parameters can be combined subject to format and hardware constraints.
For example, groupwise INT4 weights can be paired with BF16 activations. Low-precision floating-point weights with different scaling schemes use the same parameter system. This gives inference frameworks a common interface for models from different sources.
Tuning and JIT Compilation for Each Workload
The standard format provides a common representation across export formats. Preprocessing then validates parameters, pads dimensions, and repacks these tensors into layouts suited to the target kernel. Humming combines the quantization description with the weight shape, GEMM type, target GPU, and compute options to configure execution.
Three configurations describe the kernel:
Layer Config describes tensor shapes, data types, quantization parameters, and the target architecture.
Compute Config specifies the GEMM type and computation options, such as batch invariance and input scale layout.
Tuning Config selects tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, memory access, and MMA instructions. It also controls concurrency and scheduling; TMA can be configured per tensor.
By default, Humming selects tuning configurations using device-specific heuristics. It can prepare different configurations for ranges of input sizes and dispatch to the appropriate kernel at runtime.
Humming’s unified architecture makes it straightforward to tune execution parameters and select pipelines for different workloads. At small batch sizes, a multistage pipeline using asynchronous copies ( cp.async ) and MMA can outperform a pipeline built around TMA and UMMA. At larger batch sizes, TMA and UMMA can offer better throughput. Humming accommodates both execution paths within the same configuration and component framework, allowing it to select the more effective strategy for each workload.
Together, the three configurations specialize kernels compiled with NVRTC or NVCC. Compiled kernels are cached for reuse. Inference combines the selected kernel with the preprocessed weights and runtime activations.
Shared CUDA Components Across Formats and Architectures
At the CUDA level, Humming organizes task scheduling, data movement, dequantization and scaling, Tensor Core computation, and output processing into reusable components. It provides standard, warp-specialized, and dedicated UMMA pipelines. These pipelines share compatible components while using the dataflow and synchronization required by each execution strategy.
Each group of components handles a different source of variation:
Numeric processing handles quantization formats. Decoding and arithmetic components account for bit width, integer or floating-point representation, scales, and zero points. Dequantization and scaling are integrated into the kernel's computation.
Memory and compute backends handle GPU architectures. Humming selects data movement and Tensor Core implementations for the target architecture, using asynchronous copies, TMA, and multicast where supported.
Task mapping and scheduling handle dense and MoE workloads. Each GEMM type uses the appropriate scheduling logic. Scaling and bias addition can also be fused into the output stage.
JIT compilation combines these components according to the three configurations and eliminates unused implementation branches. A new format or architecture can therefore be supported by extending the relevant components. Improvements to a shared component benefit compatible configurations, reducing the duplicated development and maintenance of separate specialized kernels.
This CUDA implementation is lightweight and avoids heavyweight kernel framework dependencies, keeping JIT compilation fast as well. In our single W4A16 kernel compilation test on an H200 server with CUDA 13.4, compilation time dropped from 23.35 seconds for CUTLASS with NVCC to 1.82 seconds for Humming with NVCC or 1.88 seconds with NVRTC , with compilation caches disabled. This reduces the cost of preparing kernels for new workloads and makes iterative tuning more practical. Humming also compiles kernels in parallel during model warmup. In our tests, compiling and loading the kernels covering all supported M sizes for a single layer's GEMM takes only about 2–4 seconds , making it practical to prepare multiple specialized kernels before inference.
Performance Tuning Based on Device Parameters
Humming deeply optimizes kernels using both the GEMM configuration and device parameters. Quantization formats, matrix shapes, GPU instruction support, SM count, shared memory, and register resources all inform execution choices, turning the benefits of low-bit storage into practical inference performance.
Efficient W4A8-MXFP4 inference on existing GPUs. Architectures before Blackwell lack native MXFP4 Tensor Core support, and conventional W4A8-MXFP4 kernels can be limited by dequantization and scaling overhead at larger M. Humming addresses this with a fast MXFP4-to-INT8/FP8 dequantization path that converts MXFP4 weights into a supported compute format within the kernel. In this setting, the path substantially outperforms conventional W4A8 implementations at small M and approaches W8A8 performance at large M. GPUs such as H200 can therefore run high-performance W4A8-MXFP4 kernels while retaining the storage benefits of 4-bit weights.
Dequantization paths matched to each device. The same quantization format can benefit from different implementations across GPUs. Humming selects decoding, numeric conversion, and scaling paths for the device, pairing them with suitable memory access and compute pipelines to reduce instruction and data movement overhead. Shared components make these optimizations reusable across compatible dense and MoE kernels.
Extensive tuning controls with device-specific heuristics. Humming exposes tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, TMA, MMA instructions, CTA concurrency, and Stream-K scheduling. Device-specific heuristics combine GEMM shapes with resource constraints to balance parallelism, data reuse, and pipeline overhead, selecting different execution strategies as input sizes change. Developers can use the default configurations directly or refine them for particular models and deployment scenarios.
Results
Broad Device Support
Humming's unified architecture enables broad GPU support. For NVIDIA GPUs, Humming fully supports every architecture from Turing onward, bringing a common quantized computing framework to multiple generations of hardware.
The unified JIT architecture also makes it straightforward to extend Humming to other GPUs compatible with CUDA programming. Humming already fully supports T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, bringing its shared kernels and tuning capabilities to more hardware platforms.
The figure below shows the high-performance activation types supported by Humming on each device: types that can take full advantage of the device's peak compute capabilities. Some types omitted from the figure can still run through other instruction paths. For example, UMMA instructions on the B300 (SM103) no longer support INT8 computation, but earlier MMA instructions can still execute INT8 GEMM, with substantially lower performance.
Quantization Support
Humming's support for quantization types depends primarily on compatibility between activation and weight types. Its unified quantization representation and kernel architecture allow a wide range of integer and floating-point weight formats to work with activations at different precisions, providing flexible choices for model precision and deployment performance.
The figure below shows the weight and activation type combinations supported by Humming. Rows represent weight types, columns represent activation types, and checks indicate supported combinations. Together with the device support matrix above, it outlines the high-performance quantized computation paths available on each hardware architecture.
Humming also supports a special floating-point format with zero exponent bits, whose representable values match those of symmetric integers at the same bit width. For example, INT8 excluding -128 and float8e0m7 both represent integers from -127 to 127 . Weights in this format have the same activation type compatibility as INT weights of the same bit width. Humming automatically converts eligible symmetric integer weights to this format for faster dequantization.
The community has also uncovered two hidden capabilities in Blackwell Tensor Cores : native support for float4e0m3 and float8e3m4 , two special floating-point formats that are not exposed in the PTX type system. Humming supports these features across all Blackwell architectures, including datacenter SM100/SM103 and SM120/SM121 devices for workstations and personal computing. Both formats are integrated into its unified quantization and compute framework, providing more native compute options for low-precision inference. Rubin does not support these two hidden Tensor Core formats, so support for these native compute paths does not extend to Rubin.
Performance
The kernel microbenchmarks below, run by the vLLM community, measure GEMM performance with M covering every power of two from 1 to 8192. Kernels are fully warmed up and timed independently with a cold L2 cache, with a brief pause between samples. MoE speedups use the sum of Gateup and Down GEMM latencies. Each figure identifies its baseline, quantization formats, matrix dimensions, and software versions.
WnA16
WnA16 is one of the most versatile and widely used approaches to quantized inference. It combines low-bit weights with FP16/BF16 activations, reducing weight storage and memory traffic while making use of widely available 16-bit compute capabilities. This makes it suitable for many GPU generations and model deployment scenarios. The W4A16 family has attracted particular interest from the community and is a major focus of Humming's optimization work.
For dense W4A16, Humming matches or outperforms vLLM Marlin in most tested configurations, with substantial gains on several Hopper and Blackwell workloads. The figure below uses cuBLAS as a common baseline. At small batch sizes, Humming delivers roughly 3–4× speedups on several devices. As batch size grows, it continues to use the hardware efficiently, reaching approximately twice Marlin's performance on large-batch H200 workloads and more than three times its performance in some B300 cases.
These gains extend to MoE. Humming provides efficient Indexed and Grouped paths for workloads where tokens are distributed across experts and the amount of work per expert changes with the load. In the figure below, MXFP4 W4A16 on H20 and H200 reaches roughly twice Marlin's performance in several medium-to-large batch cases. On B300, the MXINT4 and NVFP4 paths achieve even larger gains at large batch sizes, with the Grouped path reaching approximately 5×. Results on SM120 and SM121 also show Humming outperforming Marlin and the corresponding FlashInfer implementations across a range of workloads.
Humming's optimizations also extend beyond W4A16 to other WnA16 combinations. Its shared dequantization and compute paths deliver strong performance for integer and floating-point weights at different bit widths, including INT1, INT2, INT3, and FP4 through FP8. The following figure shows broad gains across these formats at small and medium batch sizes, with the lowest-bit configurations on SM120 exceeding 5× the performance of BF16 cuBLAS. At large batch sizes on H20, multiple bit widths maintain compute efficiency close to BF16 cuBLAS. This gives models finer-grained choices among precision, storage, and throughput.
W8A8 / W4A8 / W4A4
With Hopper, FP8 W8A8 with blockwise scaling became a mainstream approach to high-performance quantized inference. Humming further improves this established compute path by optimizing data movement, scaling, and expert scheduling together. The left column below shows W8A8 results on H20 and H200. At small and medium batch sizes, Humming reaches approximately 2.6× and 2.5× the performance of DeepGEMM Contiguous, respectively, with competitive performance from both Indexed and Grouped layouts.
As more models adopt native MXFP4 weight quantization, converting the smaller weight footprint into practical inference gains becomes increasingly valuable. Humming addresses this with an efficient W4A8 path that rapidly dequantizes MXFP4 weights as they are loaded and uses FP8 Tensor Cores for computation, enabling efficient W4A8-MXFP4 execution on Hopper. The right column above keeps DeepGEMM W8A8 as the baseline. At small and medium batch sizes, Humming's W4A8 reaches approximately 4.2× baseline performance on H20 and 4.5× on H200, also substantially outperforming Humming's W8A8 results in the same figure. Reduced weight traffic translates into lower GEMM latency. FlashInfer CUTLASS W4A8 is also an implementation based on Humming's approach, while Humming's current implementation achieves better performance in the benchmarks shown here.
Blackwell adds native Tensor Core support for microscaling formats such as MXFP8 and MXFP4. From datacenter SM100/SM103 devices to SM120/SM121 devices for workstations and personal computing, Humming uses each architecture's low-precision compute capabilities to support W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4 within one kernel and tuning framework.
On B300 (SM103), Humming demonstrates substantial performance gains across all three MX format combinations. Each panel below uses DeepGEMM Contiguous at the corresponding precision as its baseline. At small and medium batch sizes, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4 reach approximately 1.25×, 1.6×, and 1.4× baseline performance, respectively, and outperform the corresponding FlashInfer implementations across many workloads. Both Indexed and Grouped paths benefit from native low-precision computation, providing efficient options for different expert layouts.
These gains also extend to SM120 and SM121. In the results below, Humming's MXFP4 × MXFP8 W4A8 and NVFP4 × NVFP4 W4A4 outperform FlashInfer CUTLASS at most tested points. On SM121 at small batch sizes, performance gains reach approximately 19% for W4A8 and 9% for W4A4; on SM120, Humming also leads across most tested sizes. The unified architecture brings these low-precision inference optimizations to more devices, extending efficient quantized computation beyond the datacenter.
End-to-End Inference Performance
Humming's W4A8 gains extend to model serving. In our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash test on eight H20 GPUs with TP=8, keeping the model's MXFP4 weights unchanged and switching MoE execution from Marlin W4A16 (BF16 activations) to Humming W4A8 (tokenwise FP8 activations) improves end-to-end throughput by approximately 14%–43% and reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by approximately 25%–32% . The throughput advantage grows with concurrency: at concurrency 64, output throughput rises from 442.37 to 633.94 tokens/s, while mean time per output token (TPOT) falls by approximately 31% .

Usage
Installation
Install Humming with pip:
pip install humming-kernels
Humming uses a CUDA compiler to generate kernels on demand. If no CUDA compiler is available on the system, choose one of the following installation options to include the compilation dependencies for your environment's CUDA major version:
pip install "humming-kernels[cu12]" # CUDA 12 pip install "humming-kernels[cu13]" # CUDA 13
Humming itself is extremely lightweight, with simple dependencies and a wheel package of only about 500 KB. On-demand compilation avoids bundling a large collection of precompiled kernels. In principle, any environment capable of running PyTorch 2.7 can also run Humming, making it easy to integrate into existing inference environments.
Using Humming in vLLM
Humming is deeply integrated into vLLM. Starting with vLLM 0.29.0, CUDA installations include Humming as a dependency, so no separate Humming installation is needed. Humming supports NVIDIA GPUs across all architectures from Turing onward (SM75 and above).
The --linear-backend and --moe-backend options select Humming as the compute backend for dense GEMM and MoE GEMM, respectively. For example, enable Humming for both with tensor parallel size 8:
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --linear-backend humming --moe-backend humming

Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal .
The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more than $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which include deals still in negotiation.
And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.
Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.
Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.
Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion , up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
Tim Fernholz
Kirsten Korosec
1:40 PM PDT · October 20, 2026
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in the third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing .
That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.
The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.
The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
During a livestreamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.
“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”
In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12- to 18-month delays in obtaining the metals that blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.
Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.
SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.
Despite those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.
Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”
More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.
This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.
