items.summary: Modal 发布 Sticky Sessions，基于 Modal Servers 让同一会话的所有请求固定路由到同一容器，用 @modal.sessioned() 装饰器配合 SDK 或 HTTP API 即可创建。
items.fullContent:
Serverless routing made sticky Skip to content
Series D: $1B in annualized run rate, new funding, and where Modal goes next. Learn more
Products
Inference Serve LLMs, image, video, and audio models, from real-time to batch Sandboxes Isolated environments for coding agents, RL rollouts, and untrusted code Training Fine-tune, run RL, and evaluate models on GPUs that spin up in seconds
Platform
Modal Infrastructure Infrastructure rebuilt for AI, from the container runtime and storage to a multi-cloud capacity pool
Tools
GPU Glossary A fast guide to GPU concepts LLM Engine Advisor Pick the right model
Resources
Blog Changelog Startup Credits Partners Slack Community
Company
About Careers Events
Featured
Scaling to 1 million concurrent sandboxes in seconds Engineering
Log in Sign up
At Modal, our serverless compute powers real-time inference, training, and batch jobs, scaling automatically with demand. Sandboxes offer a different model, containers whose lifecycles you explicitly control. A growing number of workloads require something in-between; autoscaling serverless compute that maintains continuity between requests. Consider a speech-to-text model with decoder state for an audio stream, a voice agent that holds a conversation, or a multiplayer game . For these workloads, users must come back to the same container on every reconnect for the entirety of their session.
We recently launched Sticky Sessions , built on top of our low-latency Modal Servers . Every session’s requests land on the same container. To use Sticky Sessions, just create a Modal Server with the @modal.sessioned() decorator and start the sessions with the SDK or the HTTP API :
@app.server()
@modal.sessioned()
class Server:
@modal.enter()
def start(self):
subprocess.Popen(["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"])
@app.local_entrypoint()
def main():
session = Server.sessions.start(idle_timeout=600)
headers = {"Modal-Authorization": f"Bearer {session.token}"}
print(requests.get(Server.get_url(), headers=headers).text)
Serverless with strong affinity
Modal has supported WebSockets via Web Functions for some time. However, a WebSocket connection is tied to a Function “input”, not a container—if the connection drops, a new input is created on reconnect and can land on a different container.
Stateful web UIs such as Gradio and Streamlit are workloads that need strong affinity guarantees between requests and backend containers. Every request has to reach the process that holds the user’s state. One anti-pattern workaround is setting max_containers=1 , which guarantees stickiness by giving up scaling entirely.
Modal Servers already provide a softer form of affinity ; requests that share the same Modal-Affinity-Routing-Key header are routed to the same container in a best-effort manner. The container can still be scaled down or replaced at any time, routing future requests to a different container.
Sticky Sessions provide stronger routing guarantees by ensuring all requests in the same session land on the same container.
Modal Servers gave us the foundation
Sticky Sessions build on the infrastructure we developed for Modal Servers . At the core of this infrastructure is our in-house stateless proxy (fprs). The proxy provides low-latency routing and load balancing using in-memory cached routing state reconciled from durable storage. Servers already give us a way to route HTTP traffic to a container, manage container lifecycles, and scale the fleet based on demand.
Sticky Sessions needed three things that the current request-level routing didn’t provide:
Fixed routing: Every request in a session reaches the same container.
Session lifecycle: The container’s host tracks which requests belong to which sessions and determines when each session becomes idle.
Session-based autoscaling: The container fleet scales with the number of active sessions rather than requests.
Making serverless infrastructure session-aware
From the client’s perspective, a Sticky Session works like a pipe. Once the client creates a session, every future request for that session will be directed to the same container.
This may seem simple, but Modal’s serverless infrastructure was built and optimized for the opposite idea; that individual requests are independent. In viewing Modal Servers from the perspective of sessions (rather than just requests), we had to reason about authorization, load balancing, and autoscaling from first principles.
Authorization
Modal Servers require Proxy Tokens by default. To share Sticky Sessions, you shouldn’t need to turn off authentication or pass your Proxy Token around.
Instead, each sessions.start() request returns a signed session token to grant access to that session. Sharing this token among clients lets multiple participants access the same state in a room, game, or collaborative app.
Maintaining the session-to-container mapping in the proxy would require keeping that mapping consistent through restarts and across multiple replicas. To avoid this, we encode routing metadata directly into the token. Our proxies validate the token and route requests to the container holding the session.
Load Balancing
Since we’re not storing session state in the proxy, the authoritative view of session state lives only on the host that owns the session. This means the load balancer cannot have an instantaneous global view of available capacity.
To discover available capacity, our load balancers periodically probe containers for a snapshot of their available concurrency. The load balancers then use a combination of recent routing decisions and the probed snapshots to inform container selection. This evenly distributes sessions across available containers while minimizing wasted roundtrips to containers that are out of capacity.
Autoscaling
Modal Servers autoscale on request volume, aiming to achieve a per-container request concurrency target. The request-driven autoscaler assumes that request traffic can be rebalanced evenly across the serving fleet of containers. This model works well for stateless Servers. However, Sticky Sessions behave differently in that session traffic is not movable . Each session’s traffic has to land on the same container even if traffic volume varies across sessions.
This motivated having sessions be the unit of concurrency, akin to Modal Functions with inputs. A container can be configured to run 1 or more sessions concurrently. When concurrency runs out, new sessions wait in a queue for existing sessions to end or a new container to become ready. The autoscaler continuously monitors active session counts and queued demand to make scaling decisions that appropriately size the compute fleet.
What Sticky Sessions unlock
Sticky Sessions’ strong routing and lifecycle guarantees on top of Servers enable first-class support for a new suite of applications on Modal:
Low-latency voice agents: The Modal Phonon Voice Bot runs a Pipecat agent with Gradium Phonon text-to-speech over WebRTC. Each call is a Sticky Session that is pinned to a container, so WebRTC signaling reaches the container that holds the peer connection. The session keeps the container active while the audio flows through WebRTC.
Shared rooms : Our sessioned chat room example backs each chat room with a Sticky Session. Every client that connects with the session token is routed to the same container. Each room’s messages are broadcasted to everyone in the room. Clients can drop and reconnect to the same room for the lifetime of the chat room session.
Gaming: Gaming applications keep state in memory to maintain continuity and reduce lag. Sticky Sessions support both preserving progress and hosting concurrent rooms of players.
A brave, sticky world
At Modal, we love using Modal. Amidst our quest for infinite scale and frontier performance , we find ourselves playing (a lot of) Curvytron . And of course, we host our own speedy (no more input lag excuses!) us-east deployment on Modal Servers atop Sticky Sessions.
Like many multiplayer games, Curvytron has players in a shared room competing against one another in real-time. With Sticky Sessions, players can create a room, share the game link, and play with others! Modal scales based on active room count automatically.
Try it out here!
Special thanks to Claudia Zhu, Richard Gong, Akshat Bubna, Michael Waskom, and Ben Shababo for helping shape this feature!

items.title: n8n 教程：在 NVIDIA DGX Spark 上离线运行全套 AI 工作流
items.title_en: Run your n8n AI workflows on NVIDIA DGX Spark, with no cloud API
items.summary: n8n 博客发布教程，讲解如何在一台 NVIDIA DGX Spark（128GB 统一内存）上部署七个本地模型，通过 LiteLLM 单一 OpenAI 兼容端点驱动 n8n 工作流，全程不调用云 API。
items.fullContent:
Run your n8n AI workflows on NVIDIA DGX Spark, with no cloud API – n8n Blog
Github ★ 207k Sign in Get Started
Most small businesses want the same handful of AI jobs. They want to draft emails, summarize calls, read invoices, search their own documents, and make the odd image. Plenty of them can't send customer data to a cloud API to do it.
Often the reason is data privacy and sovereignty. A clinic, a law firm, or an accountant may hold records that a contract, a regulator, or a professional duty says must stay under their control. Once that data goes to a cloud API, it sits on someone else's hardware, possibly in another jurisdiction, under terms the provider can change. Running the models on hardware you own keeps the data in your building, and lets you show an auditor exactly where it went.
Your n8n workflows can transcribe calls, read invoices, answer questions from your own documents, and draft replies without sending a byte to a cloud API. This post shows you how to serve every model those workflows need from one NVIDIA DGX Spark, behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint that n8n's OpenAI nodes already speak.
A DGX Spark has 128GB of unified memory shared by the CPU and GPU. That's enough to keep every one of those jobs loaded at once, if you pick the right models. Most of this post is about that.
The self-hosted AI starter kit gets one person running local models on a laptop. This is the next step: a box in the office that serves a whole team, with a model for each job and the code to run it.
In this post, you'll:
Choose models that run fast on the DGX Spark's memory bandwidth
Serve a 35B mixture-of-experts model with vLLM in NVFP4
Fit a full AI stack into one box's shared memory
Route every job through one LiteLLM endpoint with per-team keys
Connect n8n to the stack and build a workflow that never calls a cloud API
Measure what happens to chat speed when someone generates an image
Pick models for the bandwidth, not the parameter count
The DGX Spark's GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip reads memory at 273 GB/s. When a model generates text, it reads its active weights from memory for each token, so the fewer bytes it reads, the faster it runs.
A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model only activates a few experts per token. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has 35B parameters in total but about 3B active. Stored in NVFP4 (NVIDIA's 4-bit floating point format), those active weights are a small fraction of a dense model's.
On my DGX Spark, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B generated 120 tokens per second for one user, and 359 tokens per second in total across eight users. Those numbers include the reasoning tokens the model writes before it answers.
That gives the first design rule: one strong MoE model for everything text-shaped. Summarizing, classifying, extracting, drafting, coding, and reading screenshots all go to the same model. Every extra model is another container to pin, patch, and monitor, so a specialist model only gets a slot where an LLM can't do the job.
The stack
These are the models that stay loaded on one DGX Spark:
Job Model License Chat, coding, vision, extraction nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 Apache 2.0 Embeddings Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B Apache 2.0 Reranking Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B Apache 2.0 Speech to text openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo MIT Document OCR zai-org/GLM-OCR MIT Image generation Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo Apache 2.0 Text to speech hexgrad/Kokoro-82M Apache 2.0 Every model in the stack allows commercial use. That rule cost more than any technical one, and there's a section on it later.
Step 1: Cache everything for offline use
The stack has to run with the network cable unplugged, so download every model once and record the exact commit you got. This loop caches each model and writes a lock file of repository and commit:
pipx install "huggingface_hub[cli]"
hf auth login
for repo in nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B \
openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo zai-org/GLM-OCR Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo; do
hf download "$repo"
echo "$repo $(cat ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--${repo//\//--}/refs/main)" >> models.lock
done When you start a model, pass --revision with the commit from models.lock . vLLM then serves the weights you tested rather than whatever main points to today, so an upstream change can't swap the weights or the license under you.
Check the vLLM version, not the tag
Pin containers the same way, and check what's inside them. My first attempt used vLLM's cu130-nightly tag. That tag had stopped updating, and the image it pulled was five months old, with vLLM 0.19. It couldn't load Qwen3.6 at all. The errors didn't mention versions. They were a KeyError for a missing weight-scale parameter, which reads like a broken checkpoint.
Before you trust an image, print the vLLM version inside it:
docker run --rm --entrypoint python3 <image> -c "import vllm; print(vllm.__version__)" The image that worked was the official vllm/vllm-omni:v0.30.0 , which ships vLLM 0.30.0 with an arm64 build. vLLM-Omni is a full vLLM with extra serving modes for images and speech, so it also serves plain LLMs. Its default entrypoint isn't vllm serve , so wrap it once:
printf 'FROM vllm/vllm-omni:v0.30.0\nENTRYPOINT ["vllm", "serve"]\n' | docker build -t vllm-spark:omni-0.30.0 - The Kokoro-FastAPI image needed a community fix to build on arm64. The Dockerfile comes from a post by swann.schilling on the NVIDIA Developer Forums .
Step 2: Serve the backbone
This command starts the main model in vLLM:
docker run -d --name qwen3.6 --gpus all --ipc=host \
-p 172.17.0.1:8001:8000 \
-e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 -e VLLM_API_KEY=<your-backend-key> \
-v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
vllm-spark:omni-0.30.0 \
nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 --revision <commit-from-models.lock> \
--served-model-name qwen3.6-35b \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.32 --max-model-len 65536 \
--max-num-seqs 8 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
--trust-remote-code --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --moe-backend marlin \
--enable-chunked-prefill --async-scheduling --enable-prefix-caching \
--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3,"moe_backend":"triton"}' \
--reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 On my DGX Spark, this model was ready to serve 311 seconds after docker run .
The port is published on 172.17.0.1 , Docker's bridge address, so only containers on this machine can reach it. VLLM_API_KEY makes vLLM reject any request without the key.
The flags that matter most on a DGX Spark:
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.32 caps this model at about a third of memory. The other models need the rest.
--kv-cache-dtype fp8 halves the memory the KV cache needs, so the same budget holds more context.
--moe-backend marlin picks the kernel for the quantized expert layers. The draft model's experts aren't quantized, so --speculative-config sets its own moe_backend .
--speculative-config turns on multi-token prediction (MTP). The model drafts three tokens ahead and checks them in one pass.
--reasoning-parser and --tool-call-parser must match the model family. When tool calling fails, check these flags before you blame the model.
Check the startup log for the kernels vLLM chose. These lines are from my run:
Using MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel for NVFP4 GEMM
Using 'MARLIN' NvFp4 MoE backend out of potential backends: ['FLASHINFER_TRTLLM', 'FLASHINFER_CUTEDSL', ...]
Your GPU does not have native support for FP4 computation but FP4 quantization is being used.
Weight-only FP4 compression will be used leveraging the Marlin kernel. That last warning matters for how you read "NVFP4" on a DGX Spark. With this vLLM build, the weights are stored in 4 bits, but the math runs in 16 bits. You still get most of the benefit, because generating tokens is limited by reading weights from memory, and 4-bit weights are a quarter of the size. Faster FP4 kernels for GB10 may raise these numbers in later builds.
Step 3: Fit the rest into shared memory
On a DGX Spark, the GPU and the operating system share one 128GB pool. Linux reported 121GB of it as total memory on my box. That changes two things you might take for granted on a discrete GPU.
First, --gpu-memory-utilization is a fraction of the whole pool, taken at startup. It's not a fraction of what's free. An instance without a cap tries to take almost everything, and the next model fails to start.
Second, vLLM sizes its cache from the memory that's free when it starts. Start two models at once and they fight over the same memory. Start one at a time, and wait for each to answer its health check before starting the next:
until curl -sf http://172.17.0.1:8001/health; do sleep 5; done If a model fails with CUDA error: out of memory while free shows plenty available, the Linux page cache is holding it. This is common straight after downloading 220GB of weights. Drop the cache, then start the model again:
sudo sh -c 'sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches' This is how long each service took to load from cold, with the page cache dropped first, and how much memory it took:
Service Seconds to ready GB taken qwen3.6 237 43 rerank 106 8 whisper 136 8 ocr 137 11 image 96 20 tts 21 3 The embedding model needed one more flag on vLLM 0.30.0, --convert embed , and started later, after the rest. With all seven models loaded, the DGX Spark used 108GB and had 13GB available. That's the limit of what one DGX Spark holds. Start the stack well before anyone needs it: the six services in the table took about 12 minutes.
vLLM can also fail at startup with Error in memory profiling , when another process frees memory while vLLM measures what's available. On shared memory, that happens if another model is loading or shutting down. Start the model again once the box is quiet.
Step 4: Put one endpoint in front
LiteLLM gives every client one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Each job is a named route, so you can swap the model behind a route without touching any client. LiteLLM also handles virtual keys, teams, and budgets in its open-source version.
Each route in LiteLLM's config.yaml points at a backend. This excerpt shows three of them:
model_list:
- model_name: qwen3.6 # main model: chat, coding, vision, extraction
litellm_params:
model: hosted_vllm/qwen3.6-35b
api_base: http://host.docker.internal:8001/v1

On the independent Artificial Analysis text-to-speech leaderboards (October 2026), Ming-3.0-tts ranks 1st among open-weights models on Controlled Voice , 1st overall on Pronunciation Robustness , and 3rd among open-weights models on Provider Voice . Ranks change as new models are added.

Voice creation: clone a reference voice, design one from text, or choose from 100+ Chinese and five English built-in voices.
Free-form control: guide speech delivery with natural-language instructions.

Diffusion at Scale: Introducing Mercury 3
Inception Team
Today we’re introducing Mercury 3, the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date. Across a range of benchmarks, Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, while running 4–8x faster at 1,000+ tokens per second.
Mercury 3 demonstrates that text diffusion scales. It’s more than 40x larger than Mercury 1 and is vastly more intelligent, but just as fast.
Early-access partners already use Mercury 3 for voice and chat support, real-time tutoring, data engineering, and web navigation:
Mercury 3 at a glance
Quality: On par or better than frontier speed-optimized models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5.
Speed: 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs.
Context: 1M tokens, up from 260K for Mercury 2.5
Price: $0.20 per million input and $0.70 per million output tokens.
At launch, Mercury 3 is 50% off at $0.10 per 1M input and $0.35 per 1M output. Cached tokens are 90% off the input price.
Diffusion at scale
When we launched Mercury 1, it was the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications. The open question in the AI community was whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases.
Mercury 3 answers that question: they can. We’ve scaled Mercury more than 40x in total parameters, and intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks has risen 3x from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. The scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion too.
Mercury 3 in production
Early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 to power latency-sensitive applications such as browser use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support.
Browser Use Agents
Agents wait on the model at every step, so small delays compound quickly. Mercury keeps each pass fast, whether the agent is navigating websites, researching across sources, or analyzing logs and tracing incidents. Agents finish sooner and have time to try more approaches before answering.
We ran Mercury 3 inside our production web-agent harness against frontier models, on 50 live Mind2Web navigation tasks. Mercury 3 completed 50% of them, significantly more than GPT-6.1-Sol. It did so using the same token volume and the same number of agent steps as a frontier model, at a fraction of the per-token cost.
Shuhao Zhang, Cofounder, TinyFish AI
Interactive Education
Learning runs on fast feedback loops, and any delay pulls a student out of the material. Mercury reasons through each request and responds in near real time, whether it’s a voice tutor carrying a conversation, an assistant grading work, or an app adapting the next question to what the student just got wrong.
Mercury 3 allowed us to give every student instant feedback without giving up reasoning. Hints, marked answers and definitions now come back in about a second, with quality as good as or better than the models we ran before. When a student is stuck on a question, that speed keeps them working instead of waiting, and it was a drop-in swap for our existing stack.
Michael Tong, Co-founder/CTO, General Learning aka RevisionDojo
Real-time search agents
Search applications start to feel unresponsive after just a few seconds delay. Mercury 3 runs fast enough to process dozens of documents and still answer while the user is engaged.
On smart glasses, an answer that takes five seconds feels broken. In our Sense API tests, Octen search took about 80ms; model generation was the bottleneck. Mercury 3 delivered the best balance of speed and quality among the fast models we tested, with a median generation time of 0.9 seconds and a median end-to-end response time of 2.2 seconds.
Kuan Zou, Founder & CEO, Octen AI
Customer support
Support agents have to answer quickly, often for regulated businesses where a wrong answer is costly. Mercury keeps responses conversational without sacrificing accuracy.
At Lorikeet, we help complex and regulated businesses build a concierge for their customers that works across voice, chat and email. In chat and voice, customers need fast responses, but we can't compromise on accuracy or getting the job done correctly. In early testing, Mercury 3 beat other models on latency while also performing higher on evals and in production.
Michael Gribben, Member of Technical Staff, Lorikeet
A real-time product portfolio
Mercury 3 is the flagship model in a widening portfolio of products that enable real-time AI.
Mercury Voice: Mercury Voice is customized for the extreme low-latency requirements of voice applications and for minimizing time to first answer token (TTFAT), not just end-to-end latency. It’s already powering agents at Audivi AI, Altur, and OpenCall.
Mercury Decide: Mercury Decide is a decision model built for high-volume classification. It outperforms Jev on benchmarks including JevBench and LegalBench.
Get started
Mercury 3 is available today on the Inception API Platform and through OpenRouter, Baseten, and Vercel. It is OpenAI API compatible, so it drops into your existing stack with no rewrites. Enterprise deployments support dedicated capacity, autoscaling, compliance controls, and configurable data retention.
